사과잼.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'apple jam', combining Sino-Korean 사과 (沙果, 'apple') with the English loanword 잼 (jam).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사과잼

사다.etymology: Core native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to buy, purchase', attested unchanged in form and sense since Middle Korean 사다.

history.meaning: to buy, purchase, earn (goodwill or resentment)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사다

사다리.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'ladder', descending from Middle Korean 사ᄃᆞ리 ('wooden ladder or steps', structurally linked to 서다 'to stand/climb' + 다리 'bridge, leg').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사다리

사람.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'person, human being', descending from Middle Korean 사ᄅᆞᆷ ('person, human'), historically derived from the verb stem 살- (살다, 'to live') plus the substantive nominalizing suffix -ᄋᆞᆷ.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사람

사무소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사무소 (事務所), meaning 'office, agency, bureau', formed from 사무 (事務, 'office work, administrative business') + 소 (所, 'place, institution').

history.meaning: establishment where business or administrative affairs are handled

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사무소

사무실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사무실 (事務室), meaning 'office room, workplace', formed from 사무 (事務, 'office work, administrative duties') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사무실

사발.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사발 (沙鉢), meaning 'large ceramic bowl (for rice, soup, or traditional drinks)', formed from 沙 (사, 'sand, porcelain/earthenware') + 鉢 (발, 'bowl', originally a Buddhist transcription of Sanskrit pātra 'alms bowl').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사발

사실.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and adverb 사실 (事實), meaning 'fact, reality, truth; in fact, actually', composed of 事 (사, 'matter, affair, event') + 實 (실, 'real, true, actual').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사실

사십.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 사십 (四十), meaning 'forty (40)', formed from 四 (사, 'four') + 十 (십, 'ten').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사십

사이.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'space between, interval (of space or time), gap; relationship between people', descending from Middle Korean ᄉᆞ이 ('interval, gap, space between').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사이

사이즈.etymology: Borrowed from English size ('physical dimensions, magnitude, or standardized measurement of clothing/objects').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사이즈

사장.etymology: Sino-Korean 사장 (社長), from 사 (社, 'company, enterprise') + 장 (長, 'head, chief').
사장.notes: With honorific -님 (사장님), it is the universal polite title for shop, café, and guesthouse owners.

사장님.etymology: Combines Sino-Korean 사장 (社長, 'company president, shop proprietor') with the native honorific suffix -님.
사장님.notes: In everyday Seoul life, 사장님 politely addresses both a workplace boss and any café, restaurant, or shop owner.

사장조.etymology: Korean musical key name joining pitch letter 사 ('G', 7th of 가나다라마바사 = A–G) with Sino-Korean 장조 (長調, 'major key').
사장조.notes: Contrasts with 사단조 (g minor, 短調).

사진.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사진 (寫眞), meaning 'photograph, picture', literally 'copying the true likeness', from 寫 (사, 'depict, copy') + 眞 (진, 'truth, reality'). Used in Classical Chinese and Joseon Korea for lifelike portrait paintings before being adopted in the late 19th century for camera photography.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사진

사촌.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship term 사촌 (四寸), literally 'four joints/degrees of kinship'.
사촌.notes: Traditional Korean kinship counts degrees (촌): parents-to-child is 1, siblings are 2, aunts/uncles are 3, and first cousins are 4 (사촌).

사포질.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'sanding, smoothing a surface with sandpaper', combining Sino-Korean 사포 (沙布, 'sandpaper, emery cloth', from 沙 'sand' + 布 'cloth') with the native Korean action suffix -질 ('repetitive work with a tool').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사포질

morphemes.meaning: act of working with an implement

사포질하다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb meaning 'to sand, smooth with sandpaper', formed from 사포질 ('sanding', from 사포 沙布 'sandpaper' + -질) plus the verbalizer -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사포질하다

사호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 사호실 (四號室), meaning 'Room 4, Room No. 4', formed from 四 (사, 'four') + 號 (호, 'number, designation') + 室 (실, 'room').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사호실

사흘.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'three days (or the third day of the month)', descending from Middle Korean 사ᄒᆞᆯ ('three days'), built from the native Korean numeral root 사-/서- ('three') plus the native day-counting suffix -ᄒᆞᆯ (compare 하루, 이틀, 나흘).

history.meaning: three days; third day of the month

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 사흘

산.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 산 (山, Middle Chinese *srean*), meaning 'mountain, hill', which gradually replaced the native Middle Korean word 뫼 ('mountain') in everyday speech.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 산

산꿀.etymology: Hybrid Sino-native Korean compound joining Sino-Korean 산 (山, 'mountain') with native 꿀 ('honey').
산꿀.notes: Refers to dark, aromatic wildflower and chestnut honey harvested from mountain apiaries.

살.etymology: Core native Korean noun representing three Middle Korean words of the form 살: (1) 'flesh, muscle, skin, meat of fruit/fish'; (2) the native bound classifier for 'years of age' (etymologically connected to 살다 'to live'); and (3) 'arrow, spoke of a wheel, lattice bar, ray of light'.

history.meaning: flesh; year of age; arrow, spoke, lattice strip
flesh, skin; years old; spoke, lattice bar, ray

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살

살다.etymology: Core native Korean ㄹ-stem verb meaning 'to live, be alive, dwell, reside', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 살다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살다

살리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to save (a life), keep alive, revive; to make the most of, bring out (a feature or flavor)', derived from 살다 ('to live') plus the causative suffix -리- (Middle Korean 살리다).

history.meaning: to make live, save a life, revive
to save, keep alive, revive, highlight/bring out

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살리다

morphemes.meaning: to cause to live / bring to life

살살.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic adverb meaning 'gently, softly, lightly, carefully, little by little', formed by reduplicating the light-vowel ideophonic root 살-.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살살

살짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'slightly, lightly, gently, stealthily, just a bit', attested in Early Modern Korean as 살짝.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살짝

살펴보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to examine closely, look around carefully, check on', combining 살피다 ('to inspect, observe, look into carefully', Middle Korean ᄉᆞᆯ피다) with the auxiliary verb 보다 ('to see, try').

history.meaning: to inspect and see, examine closely
to examine, look around, check carefully

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 살펴보다

삼.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 삼 (三, Middle Chinese *sam*), meaning 'three (3)'. Also homophonous with native Korean 삼 ('hemp', Middle Korean 삼) and Sino-Korean 삼 (蔘, 'ginseng').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼

삼나무.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'cedar, Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica)', combining Sino-Korean 삼 (杉, 'cryptomeria, cedar') with native Korean 나무 ('tree, wood', Middle Korean 나모).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼나무

삼만.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 삼만 (三萬), meaning 'thirty thousand (30,000)', formed from 三 (삼, 'three') + 萬 (만, 'ten thousand').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼만

삼십.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 삼십 (三十), meaning 'thirty (30)', formed from 三 (삼, 'three') + 十 (십, 'ten').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼십

삼십오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 삼십오 (三十五), meaning 'thirty-five (35)', composed of 三 (삼, 'three') + 十 (십, 'ten') + 五 (오, 'five').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼십오

삼촌.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship compound 삼촌 (三寸), meaning 'uncle (especially father's brother)', literally 'three degrees/joints of kinship' in the traditional Korean 촌수 (寸數) system of reckoning collateral consanguinity (where parent to child is 1촌, siblings are 2촌, and a parent's sibling is 3촌).

history.meaning: third degree of kinship -> parent's brother

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼촌

삼층.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 삼층 (三層), meaning 'third floor, three stories', formed from 三 (삼, 'three') + 層 (층, 'story, floor, tier').

history.meaning: third level or story of a building

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 삼층

상봉.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상봉 (相逢), meaning 'reunion, meeting each other after separation', formed from 相 (상, 'mutually, each other') + 逢 (봉, 'meet, encounter'); also used as a place and station name in eastern Seoul (上鳳, 상봉).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상봉

상업용.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상업용 (商業用), meaning 'for commercial use, commercial-grade', formed from 상업 (商業, 'commerce, business') + suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of').

history.meaning: intended for commercial or business use

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상업용

상인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상인 (商人), meaning 'merchant, trader, shopkeeper', composed of 商 (상, 'commerce, trade') + 人 (인, 'person').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상인

상자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상자 (箱子), meaning 'box, case, chest, carton', composed of 箱 (상, 'box, chest, trunk') + nominal suffix 子 (자).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상자

상처.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 상처 (傷處), meaning 'wound, injury, scar; emotional hurt', literally 'injured place', from 傷 (상, 'wound, hurt, damage') + 處 (처, 'place, spot').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 상처

새.etymology: Core native Korean determiner meaning 'new, fresh, brand-new', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 새. Also homophonous with native Korean nouns 새 ('bird', Middle Korean 새) and 새 (contraction of 사이 'space/time between').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새

새것.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'a new thing, brand-new item', formed from the native determiner 새 ('new') + bound noun 것 ('thing, object').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새것

새기다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to carve, engrave, inscribe, etch (into wood, stone, metal, or one's heart)', descending from Middle Korean 사기다 ('to carve, engrave; to interpret') via regressive vowel fronting (사기다 > 새기다).

history.meaning: to carve, engrave, inscribe, bear in mind

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새기다

새다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb uniting two Middle Korean verbs: (1) 샏다 / 새다 ('to leak out, escape', of water, gas, light, or secrets); and (2) 새다 ('to dawn, grow bright as night ends', related to 새벽 'dawn').

history.meaning: to leak out; to break (of dawn)
to leak, escape; to dawn, stay up all night

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새다

새벽.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'dawn, daybreak, the small hours of the morning', descending from Middle Korean 새배 ('dawn, daybreak', formed from the root 새- 'to dawn, grow light' + 밝-/배 'bright, morning').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새벽

새소리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'birdsong, chirping or singing of birds', formed from 새 ('bird') + 소리 ('sound, voice').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새소리

새하얗다.etymology: Native Korean intensifying colour prefix 새- ('vividly, dazzlingly') + 하얗다 ('white').

새하얘지다.etymology: Native Korean compound inchoative verb meaning 'to become dazzlingly/pure white, turn pale', formed from the intensified color adjective 새하얗다 (prefix 새- 'vividly, completely' + 하얗다 'white') plus the inchoative auxiliary -어지다 (새하얗- + -어지다 -> 새하얘지다).

history.meaning: to turn pure white, become snow-white

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 새하얘지다

색깔.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'color, hue, tint', formed from Sino-Korean 색 (色, 'color') plus the native Korean bound element -깔 (tensified from 갈 'quality, aspect, look', seen also in 빛깔 'hue', 맛깔 'savory quality', and 성깔 'temper').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 색깔

생각.etymology: Korean noun meaning 'thought, idea, opinion, memory, intention', attested since Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각 (traditionally traced to a nativized Sino-Korean compound 生覺, 'arising of awareness/perception', from 生 'arise' + 覺 'perceive, realize').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생각

생각하다.etymology: Verb meaning 'to think, consider, ponder, remember', formed from 생각 ('thought, idea', Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ각) plus the verbalizer -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생각하다

생기다.etymology: Intransitive verb meaning 'to come into being, form, arise, occur, be acquired; to look a certain way', attested from Middle Korean ᄉᆡᆼ기다 (built on Sino-Korean 生 'be born, arise' or native 살-/ᄉᆡᆼ- plus the native suffix -기다).

history.meaning: to be formed, come into existence
to arise, happen, be formed; to look (a certain way)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생기다

생나무.etymology: Hybrid compound combining Sino-Korean prefix 생- (生, 'raw, unseasoned, bare') with native 나무 ('tree, wood').
생나무.notes: Refers either to freshly cut green timber or to bare wood with no lacquer or paint.

생음악.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 생음악 (生音樂), meaning 'live music (performed in person rather than played from a recording)', formed from the prefix 생- (生, 'live, raw, direct') + 음악 (音樂, 'music').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생음악

생지.etymology: Sino-Korean culinary and craft term 생지 (生地), meaning 'unbaked pastry dough, raw dough (or unbleached cloth / unfired clay body)', adopted via the Sino-Korean reading of Japanese 生地 (kiji, 'raw material, unbaked dough'), from 生 (생, 'raw, unworked') + 地 (지, 'ground, base material').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 생지

샤워.etymology: Borrowed from English shower ('bath in which water is sprayed from overhead').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 샤워

샤워기.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'showerhead, shower fixture', combining the English loanword 샤워 (shower) with Sino-Korean 기 (器 / 機, 'apparatus, fixture, device').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 샤워기

서다.etymology: Core native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to stand, stand up; to stop, come to a halt; to be erected or established', descending from Middle Korean 셔다 ('to stand') via regular loss of the palatal glide after ㅅ.

history.meaning: to stand; to stop/halt; to be set up

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서다

서두르다.etymology: Native Korean 르-irregular verb meaning 'to hurry, rush, hasten, make haste', descending from Early Modern Korean 셔두르다 / 서두르다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서두르다

서랍.etymology: Korean noun meaning 'drawer (of a desk, table, or chest)', descending from Early Modern Korean 셜합 / 설합 (舌盒, literally 'tongue-like sliding box', from 舌 'tongue' + 盒 'covered box') through liquid-aspirate simplification (설합 > 서랍).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서랍

서류.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서류 (書類), meaning 'documents, papers, official paperwork', formed from 書 (서, 'writing, document') + 類 (류, 'category, class, collection').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서류

서류철.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서류철 (書類綴), meaning 'document binder, file folder', formed from 서류 (書類, 'documents, papers') + 철 (綴, 'bind together, stitch, file').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서류철

서른다섯.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral meaning 'thirty-five (35)', combining 서른 ('thirty', Middle Korean 설흔) + 다섯 ('five', Middle Korean 다ᄉᆞᆺ).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서른다섯

서명.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서명 (署名), meaning 'signature, autograph, signing one's name', composed of 署 (서, 'write down, sign, public office') + 名 (명, 'name').

history.meaning: writing one's name on a document

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서명

서비스.etymology: Borrowed from English service ('assistance or work provided to customers'; in South Korean restaurant and retail usage, also extended to mean 'a complimentary item or dish on the house').

history.meaning: work or assistance performed for customers

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서비스

서울.etymology: Native Korean proper name meaning 'capital city', widely connected by historical linguists through Middle Korean 셔ᄫᅳᆯ (syeweul) to Old Korean 서라벌 (Seorabeol), the capital of Silla.
서울.notes: Uniquely among East Asian capitals, 서울 is a native vernacular word rather than a Sino-Korean character compound.

서재.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 서재 (書齋), meaning 'study, private library, reading room', formed from 書 (서, 'book, writing') + 齋 (재, 'study room, quiet studio').

history.meaning: scholar's room for reading and writing

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 서재

선명하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 선명 (鮮明, 선 'fresh, vivid' + 명 'bright, clear') + -하다.
선명하다.notes: Describes vivid paint colours, sharp photographs, or crisp lettering.

선반.etymology: Sino-Korean-derived noun 선반 (懸板 / 宣盤), meaning 'shelf, ledge, rack mounted on a wall or inside a cabinet', attested in Early Modern Korean as 션반.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 선반

선생님.etymology: Hybrid respectful title combining Sino-Korean 선생 (先生, literally 'born earlier', i.e. teacher/elder) with the native Korean honorific suffix -님.
선생님.notes: Addresses teachers, doctors, and respected older guests warmly and politely.

선택.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 선택 (選擇), meaning 'choice, selection, option', composed of two synonymous morphemes: 選 (선, 'choose, select') + 擇 (택, 'pick out, select').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 선택

선풍기.etymology: Sino-Korean 선풍기 (扇風機), combining 선 (扇, 'fan') + 풍 (風, 'wind') + 기 (機, 'machine').
선풍기.notes: Pronounced [선풍기]; contrasts with 부채 (handheld paper/bamboo fan).

설계도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 설계도 (設計圖), meaning 'blueprint, architectural or engineering design plan', formed from 설계 (設計, 'design, plan') + 도 (圖, 'drawing, diagram, chart').

history.meaning: diagram or blueprint of a planned structure

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설계도

설계하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 설계 (設計, 'design, planning, layout', from 設 'set up, establish' + 計 'calculate, plan') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to plan and lay out a structure or system

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설계하다

설마.etymology: Native Korean modal adverb expressing strong doubt or disbelief ('surely not, no way, could it possibly be that...'), descending from Middle Korean 셜마.

history.meaning: surely not, by no means, no way

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설마

설명하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 설명 (說明, 'explanation, elucidation', literally 'speaking to make clear') plus verbalizer -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 설명하다

설탕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 설탕 (雪糖), literally 'snow sugar', from 설 (雪, 'snow') and 당/탕 (糖, 'sugar').
설탕.notes: Named for the fine white crystals of refined sugar resembling fresh snow.

성민.etymology: Common Korean given name 성민, typically written with Sino-Korean hanja combinations such as 成民 ('accomplished among the people') or 聖旼 ('wise and gentle').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 성민

성함.etymology: Sino-Korean honorific compound 성함 (姓銜), meaning 'esteemed name (polite/honorific word for another person's name)', formed from 姓 (성, 'surname, family name') + 銜 (함, 'official title, respected name').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 성함

세.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral meaning 'three (3)' used before nouns and classifiers (e.g., 세 개, 세 번), derived by pre-consonantal final drop from 셋 ('three', Middle Korean 세ㅎ / 셋). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 세 (歲 'years of age'; 貰 'rent').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세

세다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'strong, powerful, forceful, intense', descending from Middle Korean 셰다 ('strong, fierce'). Also homophonous with native Korean verbs 세다 ('to count', from Middle Korean 헤다) and 세다 ('to turn gray/white of hair', from Middle Korean 싀다).

history.meaning: to be strong; to count; to turn white
strong, powerful, intense; to count; to turn gray

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세다

세상.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 세상 (世上), meaning 'the world, society, life among people', composed of 世 (세, 'world, age, generation') + 上 (상, 'upon, realm').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세상

세우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to make stand, erect, build, set up; to stop or park (a vehicle); to establish (a plan or rule)', descending from Middle Korean 셰우다 / 세오다 (causative of 셔다 > 서다 'to stand').

history.meaning: to stand up, erect, build, stop (a car), form (a plan)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세우다

세워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb meaning 'to be erected, be built, be established, be set up', formed from the causative verb 세우다 ('to erect, set up') plus the passive/inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세워지다

세월.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 세월 (歲月), meaning 'time, years and months, the flow of time', composed of 歲 (세, 'year') + 月 (월, 'month').

history.meaning: years and months -> the passage of time

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 세월

센터.etymology: Borrowed from English center / centre ('central point; facility or organization dedicated to a particular activity or service').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 센터

센티미터.etymology: Borrowed from English centimeter / centimetre ('one hundredth of a meter, cm', from French centimètre).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 센티미터

셋.etymology: Core native Korean numeral meaning 'three (3)', descending from Middle Korean 셋 / 세ㅎ ('three').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셋

셋째.etymology: Native Korean ordinal numeral and noun meaning 'third (3rd); the third child', formed from 셋 ('three', Middle Korean 셋) plus the native ordinal suffix -째.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셋째

셔츠.etymology: Borrowed from English shirt / shirts ('collared upper-body garment with sleeves', entered via the plural form shirts).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셔츠

셔터.etymology: Borrowed from English shutter ('rolling metal security door over a shopfront or window; mechanical or electronic camera shutter').

history.meaning: hinged or rolling cover for an opening; camera shutter

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셔터

셰프님.etymology: Hybrid honorific noun meaning 'Chef (respectful title of address or reference)', combining the French/English loanword 셰프 (chef, 'head cook') with the native Korean honorific suffix -님.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 셰프님

소금.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'salt', descending from Middle Korean 소곰 ('salt') through unrounding/delabialization of the second-syllable vowel (소곰 > 소금).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소금

소라.etymology: Korean female given name 소라, homonymous with the native Korean noun 소라 ('horned turban shell, conch', attested since Middle Korean 소라).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소라

소리.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'sound, voice, noise, song, remark', descending from Middle Korean 소리 ('sound, voice').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소리

소리치다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to shout, yell, cry out loudly', formed from 소리 ('loud voice, cry') + 치다 ('to strike, utter or emit forcefully').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소리치다

소매.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'sleeve (of a garment)', descending from Middle Korean 소매 ('sleeve', historically linked to 손 'hand, arm' + -매). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 소매 (小賣, 'retail sale').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소매

소박하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 소박 (素朴, 'simple, plain, unadorned, artless', from 素 'uncolored silk, plain' + 朴 'unworked wood, honest') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: plain and unpretentious like unworked wood

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소박하다

소식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소식 (消息), meaning 'news, word, tidings, update', from 消 (소, 'wane, disappear') + 息 (식, 'wax, grow, breathe'), which in Classical Chinese meant 'waxing and waning of things, how matters stand' and hence 'news of someone's condition'.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소식

소유권.etymology: Sino-Korean legal compound 소유권 (所有權), meaning 'ownership, property right, legal title', formed from 소유 (所有, 'possession, ownership') + 권 (權, 'right, authority').

history.meaning: legal right to possess and dispose of property

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소유권

소음.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 소음 (騷音), meaning 'noise, din, unwanted or disruptive sound', formed from 騷 (소, 'disturb, commotion, uproar') + 音 (음, 'sound').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소음

소중하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 소중 (所重, literally 'that which is held weighty or dear') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: held in high regard or importance

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 소중하다

속.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'inside, interior, core; stomach; inner mind or feelings', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 속.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 속

손.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'hand; manual effort, labor, help', descending unchanged from Middle Korean 손. Also homophonous with native Korean 손 ('guest, visitor; wandering spirit', Middle Korean 손, the root of 손님).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손

손가락.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound of 손 ('hand') and 가락 ('slender stick, spindle, or digit').
손가락.notes: The same native element 가락 appears in 발가락 ('toe'), 젓가락 ('chopsticks'), and 숟가락 ('spoon').

손글씨.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 손 ('hand') and 글씨 ('written letters, handwriting', derived from 글 'writing').
손글씨.notes: Contrasts personal pen-and-pencil script with printed type.

손길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'touch or movement of a hand; helping hand, care', formed from 손 ('hand') + 길 ('way, path, course of movement').

history.meaning: touch of a hand, helping hand

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손길

손님.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'guest, visitor, customer, passenger', formed from native Korean 손 ('guest, visitor', Middle Korean 손) plus the honorific suffix -님.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손님

손대다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb meaning 'to touch, lay a hand on, start working on, meddle with', formed from 손 ('hand') + 대다 ('to bring into contact, touch').

history.meaning: to touch, lay hands on, begin or dabble in

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손대다

손뼉.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'palm of the hand, flat of the hand (especially when clapping, as in 손뼉을 치다)', descending from Middle Korean 손벽 (from 손 'hand' + 벽 'flat surface', with tensification [손뼉] reflected in modern spelling).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손뼉

손자.etymology: Sino-Korean kinship compound 손자 (孫子), meaning 'grandson', composed of 孫 (손, 'grandchild, descendant') + 子 (자, 'son, child').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손자

손잡이.etymology: Native Korean synthetic compound from 손 ('hand') + 잡- ('grip, hold') + nominalizing suffix -이: literally 'hand-holder'.
손잡이.notes: Covers door handles, suitcase handles, and teacup handles alike.

손전등.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'flashlight, hand-held electric torch', combining native Korean 손 ('hand') with Sino-Korean 전등 (電燈, 'electric light/lamp', from 電 'electricity' + 燈 'lamp').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 손전등

솔솔.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic adverb meaning 'gently, softly, smoothly (of a cool breeze blowing, a pleasant scent wafting, powder sprinkling, or water trickling)', formed by reduplicating the light-vowel ideophone 솔-.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔솔

솔직하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 솔직 (率直, 'frank, candid, honest, straightforward', from 率 'unreserved, direct' + 直 'straight, upright') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔직하다

솔직해지다.etymology: Hybrid compound inchoative verb meaning 'to become honest/frank, open up candidly', formed from the Sino-Korean adjective 솔직하다 ('frank, honest', stem 솔직해-) plus the native Korean inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔직해지다

솔직히.etymology: Hybrid adverb meaning 'frankly, honestly, candidly', formed from Sino-Korean 솔직 (率直, 'frank, straightforward') plus the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 솔직히

쇠.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'iron, metal', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 쇠 ('iron, metal, ore').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쇠

쇠걸쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'iron latch, metal hook or catch (on a door, window, or box)', formed from 쇠 ('iron, metal') + 걸쇠 ('latch, hook', itself a compound of 걸다 'to hang/hook' + 쇠 'metal fixture').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쇠걸쇠

쇠고리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'iron ring, metal loop or eye', formed from 쇠 ('iron, metal') + 고리 ('ring, loop', Middle Korean 고리).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쇠고리

수.etymology: Polysemous Korean noun: (1) native Korean bound noun 수 ('way, method, possibility, ability', used in -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 'can / cannot', descending from Middle Korean 수 'means, way'); (2) Sino-Korean 수 (數, 'number, count, quantity; fate, luck'); and (3) Sino-Korean 수 (手, 'move in a game, skill, means').

history.meaning: way, possibility (-ㄹ 수 있다); number (數); move/skill (手)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수

수건.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수건 (手巾), meaning 'towel, hand towel, cloth', composed of 手 (수, 'hand') + 巾 (건, 'cloth, kerchief, towel').

history.meaning: cloth for wiping the hands or face

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수건

수고하다.etymology: Verb meaning 'to work hard, take pains, go to trouble', formed from 수고 ('hard work, trouble, effort', attested in Middle Korean as 수고 and traditionally linked to Sino-Korean 受苦, 'undergoing toil/hardship') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to work hard, take trouble (used in thanks/greetings)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수고하다

수도.etymology: Sino-Korean compound representing two common homophones: (1) 수도 (水道), meaning 'waterworks, running water system, water conduit' (from 水 'water' + 道 'channel, way'); and (2) 수도 (首都), meaning 'capital city' (from 首 'head, chief' + 都 'metropolis').

history.form: 水道 (water supply) / 首都 (capital city)

history.meaning: running water, waterworks (水道); capital city (首都)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수도

수도관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수도관 (水道管), meaning 'water pipe, water main, plumbing pipe', formed from 수도 (水道, 'water supply, water conduit') + 관 (管, 'pipe, tube').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수도관

수도꼭지.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'faucet, water tap, spigot', combining Sino-Korean 수도 (水道, 'running water system') with native Korean 꼭지 ('knob, spout, stem, tip', Middle Korean 곡지).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수도꼭지

수상하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 수상 (殊常, literally 'different from the ordinary, unusual') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다, meaning 'suspicious, fishy, questionable, strange'.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수상하다

수성.etymology: Sino-Korean 수성 (水性), compounding 수 (水, 'water') + 성 (性, 'nature, property').
수성.notes: Used before 페인트 ('water-based paint') and 펜 ('water-based ink pen').

수수께끼.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in early modern Korean texts in forms such as 수수격기, meaning a verbal riddle or puzzle.
수수께끼.notes: Used both for word riddles and figuratively for a mysterious note or situation.

수습.etymology: Sino-Korean compound representing two common homophones: (1) 수습 (收拾), meaning 'bringing a situation under control, settling, sorting out, clearing up' (from 收 'gather' + 拾 'pick up, put in order'); and (2) 수습 (修習), meaning 'probation, apprenticeship, practical training' (from 修 'cultivate' + 習 'practice').

history.form: 收拾 (settling/sorting out) / 修習 (probationary training)

history.meaning: remedying/controlling a situation (收拾); probation/training (修習)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수습

수업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수업 (授業), meaning 'class, lesson, academic instruction', composed of 授 (수, 'confer, impart, teach') + 業 (업, 'study, coursework').

history.meaning: imparting instruction in a course of study

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수업

수요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수요일 (水曜日), meaning 'Wednesday', formed from 수요 (水曜, 'the planet Mercury, the Water Star' in traditional East Asian seven-luminary astronomy) + 일 (日, 'day').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수요일

수첩.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 수첩 (手帖), combining 수 (手, 'hand') and 첩 (帖, 'folded booklet, register').
수첩.notes: Literally a 'hand-booklet' small enough to slip into a coat or apron pocket.

수프.etymology: Borrowed from English soup ('savory liquid dish made by simmering ingredients in stock or water').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수프

수프용.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'for soup, soup-use (e.g., a soup bowl or soup spoon)', combining the English loanword 수프 (soup) with the Sino-Korean suffix -용 (用, 'for the use of').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 수프용

숙박.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박 (宿泊), meaning 'lodging, staying overnight, accommodation', composed of 宿 (숙, 'stay overnight, lodge') + 泊 (박, 'moor, stay for the night').

history.meaning: staying overnight at an inn or lodging

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숙박

숙박부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박부 (宿泊簿), from 숙박 (宿泊, 'lodging overnight') and 부 (簿, 'ledger, register book').
숙박부.notes: Shares 부 (簿, 'record book') with 장부 (帳簿, 'account ledger').

숙박비.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙박비 (宿泊費), meaning 'lodging expenses, cost of accommodation', formed from 숙박 (宿泊, 'overnight lodging') + 비 (費, 'cost, expense, fee').

history.meaning: fee or expense for overnight lodging

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숙박비

숙소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숙소 (宿所), meaning 'lodging, quarters, accommodation, place to stay', formed from 宿 (숙, 'lodge, stay overnight') + 所 (소, 'place').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숙소

순간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 순간 (瞬間), from 순 (瞬, 'blink of an eye') and 간 (間, 'interval of time').
순간.notes: Literally 'the space of a single blink'.

순전히.etymology: Hybrid adverb meaning 'purely, entirely, wholly, solely', formed from Sino-Korean 순전 (純全, 'pure and complete', from 純 'pure, unmixed' + 全 'whole, entire') plus the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 순전히

숟가락.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'spoon', descending from Middle Korean 술가락, formed from 술 ('spoon; spoonful', Middle Korean 술) + 가락 ('slender stick, rod, or utensil', Middle Korean 가락), with pre-consonantal coronal neutralization spelled ㄷ in Modern Korean orthography.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숟가락

숨.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'breath, respiration', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 숨.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨

숨겨지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb meaning 'to be hidden, be concealed', formed from the causative/transitive verb 숨기다 ('to hide, conceal', stem 숨겨-) plus the passive/inchoative auxiliary verb -어지다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨겨지다

숨기다.etymology: Native Korean causative/transitive verb meaning 'to hide, conceal, keep secret', derived from the intransitive verb 숨다 ('to hide oneself') plus the causative suffix -기- (Middle Korean 숨기다).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨기다

숨다.etymology: Core native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to hide oneself, go into hiding, lurk out of sight', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 숨다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숨다

숫자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 숫자 (數字), meaning 'number, numeral, figure, digit', formed from 數 (수, 'number, count') + 字 (자, 'character, symbol'), written in South Korean orthography with the genitive interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) as one of the six exceptional two-hanja words that take 사이시옷 (곳간, 셋방, 숫자, 찻간, 툇간, 횟수).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숫자

숲.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'forest, woods, grove', descending from Middle Korean 수플 ('woods, thicket', historically related to 숳 'thicket' + 풀 'vegetation') via syncope/apocope of the final syllable into an aspirated labial stop (수플 > 숖 > 숲).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 숲

쉬다.etymology: Native Korean verb uniting two Middle Korean verbs: (1) 쉬다 ('to rest, take a break, relax; to breathe', as in 숨을 쉬다 'to draw breath'); and (2) 싀다 > 쉬다 ('to go sour or spoil of food; to become hoarse of the voice').

history.meaning: to rest, breathe; to turn sour or hoarse
to rest, take time off; to breathe; to spoil/go sour; to get hoarse

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쉬다

쉽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'easy, simple, effortless; likely/apt to', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 쉽다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쉽다

슈거파우더.etymology: Compound loanword from English sugar and powder ('finely ground confectioners' sugar or icing sugar dusted over pastries and desserts').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 슈거파우더

스무.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral meaning 'twenty (20)' used before nouns and classifiers (e.g., 스무 살 'twenty years old', 스무 개 'twenty items'), derived by regular pre-consonantal final ㄹ loss from 스물 ('twenty', Middle Korean 스믈).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스무

스물.etymology: Core native Korean numeral meaning 'twenty (20)', descending from Middle Korean 스믈 ('twenty') via Early Modern Korean labial vowel rounding of ㅡ to ㅜ after ㅁ.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물

스물네.etymology: Native Korean compound adnominal numeral meaning 'twenty-four (24)' used before nouns and classifiers, combining 스물 ('twenty') + 네 (adnominal form of 넷 'four').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물네

스물다섯.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral meaning 'twenty-five (25)', combining 스물 ('twenty', Middle Korean 스믈) + 다섯 ('five', Middle Korean 다ᄉᆞᆺ).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물다섯

스물여덟째.etymology: Native Korean compound ordinal numeral meaning 'twenty-eighth (28th)', formed from 스물 ('twenty') + 여덟 ('eight', Middle Korean 여듧) + ordinal suffix -째.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스물여덟째

스웨터.etymology: Borrowed from English sweater ('knitted garment worn on the upper body').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스웨터

스위치.etymology: Borrowed from English switch ('device for making and breaking an electrical connection').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스위치

스크램블드에그.etymology: Compound loanword from English scrambled eggs ('dish of beaten eggs gently stirred while cooking in a pan').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스크램블드에그

스탠드.etymology: Borrowed from English stand ('upright support or holder; desk lamp or floor lamp; spectator stands').

history.meaning: upright support, lamp stand, stadium seating

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스탠드

스펀지.etymology: Borrowed from English sponge ('soft, porous, water-absorbent pad used for cleaning, baking, or cushioning'), ultimately from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스펀지

스푼.etymology: Borrowed from English spoon ('utensil with a small shallow bowl on a handle, used for eating, stirring, or measuring').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 스푼

슬쩍.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb meaning 'stealthily, discreetly, lightly, casually in passing', an intensified counterpart of 슬적.

history.meaning: quietly, discreetly, with a light motion

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 슬쩍

슬프다.etymology: Native Korean 으-irregular adjective meaning 'sad, sorrowful, mournful', descending from Middle Korean 슬프다, derived from the verb stem 슳- (슳다, 'to grieve, feel sorrow') plus the adjective-forming suffix -브다 (> -프다 after final ㅎ).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 슬프다

습기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 습기 (濕氣), meaning 'moisture, dampness, humidity', composed of 濕 (습, 'wet, damp, moist') + 氣 (기, 'air, vapor').

history.meaning: moist vapor or dampness in the air

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 습기

승강장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 승강장 (乘降場), meaning 'platform, boarding and alighting area (at a train, subway, or bus station)', formed from 승강 (乘降, 'boarding and alighting') + 장 (場, 'place, area').

history.meaning: place for getting on and off vehicles

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 승강장

승진시키다.etymology: Hybrid causative verb meaning 'to promote (someone to a higher rank or office)', combining Sino-Korean 승진 (昇進, 'promotion, advancement in rank', from 昇 'rise' + 進 'advance') with the native Korean causative verb -시키다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 승진시키다

승진하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verbal compound joining 승진 (昇進, from 昇 'ascend, rise' + 進 'advance') with native light verb -하다.
승진하다.notes: Used seriously for workplace promotions and playfully for 'getting promoted' to taste tester.

시.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and bound classifier representing three everyday homophones: (1) 시 (時, Middle Chinese *dzyi*), bound counter for 'hour, o'clock' and noun 'time'; (2) 시 (市, Middle Chinese *dzyijX*), 'city, municipality'; and (3) 시 (詩, Middle Chinese *syi*), 'poem, poetry'.

history.meaning: o'clock, hour (時); city (市); poem, poetry (詩)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시

시간.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시간 (時間), from 시 (時, 'time, hour') and 간 (間, 'interval, space between').
시간.notes: Means both 'time' in general and a duration of hours when preceded by a native Korean number (두 시간, 'two hours').

시간표.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 시간표 (時間表): 시간 ('time') + 표 (表, 'chart, table').
시간표.notes: Used for train timetables, bus schedules, and school class schedules.

시계.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시계 (時計), literally 'time-measurer', from 시 (時, 'time') + 계 (計, 'measure, gauge').
시계.notes: Covers both wall clocks and wristwatches.

시계탑.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시계탑 (時計塔), meaning 'clock tower', formed from 시계 (時計, 'clock, timepiece', from 時 'time' + 計 'measure') + 탑 (塔, 'tower, pagoda').

history.meaning: tower fitted with a large clock

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시계탑

시끄럽다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'noisy, loud, clamorous, boisterous', attested in Early Modern Korean as 식그럽다 / 시끄럽다 (built on an ideophonic/expressive stem 시끌- + adjective suffix -업다/-럽다).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시끄럽다

시나몬.etymology: Borrowed from English cinnamon ('aromatic inner bark of Cinnamomum trees used as a culinary spice', alongside Sino-Korean 계피 桂皮).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시나몬

시내.etymology: Korean noun representing two distinct etymologies: (1) Sino-Korean 시내 (市內, pronounced with a long initial vowel [시:내]), meaning 'downtown, city center, within the city' (from 市 'city' + 內 'inside'); and (2) native Korean 시내, meaning 'stream, brook, creek' (descending unchanged from Middle Korean 시내).

history.form: 市內 (within the city) / 시내 (brook, stream)

history.meaning: downtown, city center (市內); stream, brook

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시내

시럽.etymology: Borrowed from English syrup ('thick sweet liquid made by dissolving sugar in water or fruit juice'), ultimately from Medieval Latin sirupus and Arabic شراب (sharāb, 'beverage, sweet drink').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시럽

시설.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시설 (施設), meaning 'facility, installation, equipment, institution', composed of 施 (시, 'carry out, put in place') + 設 (설, 'establish, set up').

history.meaning: setting up and equipping an installation

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시설

시식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시식 (試食), from 시 (試, 'test, try') and 식 (食, 'eat, food').
시식.notes: Parallel to 시음 (試飮, 'drink tasting') and 시연 (試演, 'trial performance').

시원하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'cool, refreshing (of air, wind, or a hot broth that brings relief); relieving, satisfying, unhindered', attested in Early Modern Korean as 시원ᄒᆞ다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시원하다

시작.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시작 (始作), meaning 'beginning, start, commencement', formed from 始 (시, 'begin, initial') + 作 (작, 'make, do, undertake').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시작

시작되다.etymology: Hybrid passive/intransitive verb meaning 'to begin, be started, commence', formed from Sino-Korean 시작 (始作, 'beginning, start') plus the native Korean passive/inchoative verb -되다 ('to become, be done').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시작되다

시작하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb meaning 'to begin, start, commence', formed from 시작 (始作, 'beginning, start') plus the verbalizer -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시작하다

시장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시장 (市場), meaning 'market, marketplace, bazaar', formed from 市 (시, 'market, city') + 場 (장, 'place, ground'). Also homophonous with 시장 (市長, 'mayor of a city') and 시장 (腸, 'feeling of hunger').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시장

시청.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 시청 (市廳), from 시 (市, 'city, municipality') and 청 (廳, 'government hall, administrative office').
시청.notes: In Seoul, 시청 refers both to City Hall itself and the major subway junction beside Seoul Plaza.

시키다.etymology: Native Korean transitive and causative verb meaning 'to make or have someone do something; to order (food, drinks, or goods)', descending from Middle Korean 시키다 / 시기다 ('to cause to do, command').

history.meaning: to cause someone to do, instruct
to make/let do, order (a meal or delivery)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시키다

시트.etymology: Borrowed from English sheet ('bedsheet, baking/parchment sheet, flat layer of material') and English seat ('chair or vehicle seat').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시트

시합하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 시합 (試合, 'match, bout, game, contest', from 試 'test, try' + 合 'come together, bout') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to meet and test skill in a match
to compete in a match, have a game/bout

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시합하다

시험하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 시험 (試驗, 'test, examination, trial, experiment', from 試 'try, test' + 驗 'verify, examine') plus verbalizer -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 시험하다

식구.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식구 (食口), meaning 'family member, household member, fellow member of a close group', literally 'mouths that eat together under one roof', from 食 (식, 'eat, meals') + 口 (구, 'mouth, person').

history.meaning: mouths sharing meals in a household

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식구

식다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb meaning 'to cool down, grow cold (of hot food, liquid, or enthusiasm)', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 식다.

history.meaning: to cool, get cold, subside (of passion)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식다

식당.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식당 (食堂), meaning 'restaurant, dining hall, cafeteria, dining room', composed of 食 (식, 'eat, meal, food') + 堂 (당, 'hall, building, room').

history.meaning: hall or room for taking meals

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식당

식빵.etymology: Hybrid compound prefixing Sino-Korean 식- (食, 'meal, staple food') to 빵 ('bread', borrowed via Japanese pan from Portuguese pão).
식빵.notes: Refers specifically to an unsweetened rectangular loaf sliced for toast or sandwiches.

식사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식사 (食事), meaning 'meal, dining', composed of 食 (식, 'eat, food') + 事 (사, 'matter, act, business').

history.meaning: act or affair of taking a meal

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식사

식초.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식초 (食醋), from 식 (食, 'edible, food') and 초 (醋, 'vinegar, sour liquor').
식초.notes: Adding 식 (食) clarifies culinary vinegar in spoken Korean.

식탁.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식탁 (食卓), meaning 'dining table, kitchen table', composed of 食 (식, 'meal, food') + 卓 (탁, 'table, desk').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식탁

식탁보.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 식탁보 (食卓褓), meaning 'tablecloth', formed from 식탁 (食卓, 'dining table') + 보 (褓, 'cloth cover, wrapping cloth', also the base of 보자기).

history.meaning: cloth covering for a dining table

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식탁보

식히다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb meaning 'to cool (something) down, let cool', derived from the intransitive verb 식다 ('to cool down') plus the causative suffix -히- (Middle Korean 식히다 / 시기다).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식히다

식힘망.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'cooling rack (wire mesh rack used to cool freshly baked bread or pastries)', combining the native Korean verbal noun 식힘 ('cooling', from 식히다 'to cool' + nominalizer -ㅁ) with Sino-Korean 망 (網, 'net, wire mesh').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 식힘망

신고.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신고 (申告), meaning 'report, declaration, formal notification (to police, government, or authorities)', composed of 申 (신, 'state, report to a superior') + 告 (고, 'inform, declare').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신고

신기하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 신기 (神奇, 'marvellous, wondrous, strange and fascinating', from 神 'miraculous, divine' + 奇 'unusual, curious') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신기하다

신다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to put on, wear (shoes, boots, slippers, or socks on the feet)', descending unchanged in form from Middle Korean 신다 (verbal counterpart of the noun 신 'footwear').

history.meaning: to put on / wear (shoes or socks)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신다

신문지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신문지 (新聞紙), adding 지 (紙, 'paper') to 신문 (新聞, literally 'newly heard things' -> 'newspaper').
신문지.notes: Distinguishes physical sheets of newsprint (used for wrapping pottery or vegetables) from 신문 as a publication.

신발.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'shoes, footwear', formed from 신 ('shoe, footwear', Middle Korean 신) + 발 ('foot', or collective suffix -발).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신발

신선하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 신선 (新鮮, 'fresh, crisp, new', from 新 'new' + 鮮 'fresh, bright') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신선하다

신입.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 신입 (新入), meaning 'newcomer, new entrant, new employee or student', composed of 新 (신, 'new') + 入 (입, 'enter').

history.meaning: newly entering an organization or school

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 신입

실내.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실내 (室內), meaning 'indoors, inside a room, interior', composed of 室 (실, 'room, chamber') + 內 (내, 'inside, interior', pronounced [실래] by liquidization).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실내

실례.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실례 (失禮), literally 'losing courtesy' or 'a breach of etiquette'.
실례.notes: Pronounced [실례] by liquidization of ㄴ+ㄹ -> ㄹ+ㄹ; used in 실례합니다 and 실례지만 ('excuse me').

실례하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb formed from 실례 (失禮, 'breach of etiquette, rudeness, excusing oneself', literally 'losing courtesy', from 失 'lose' + 禮 'courtesy') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to commit a breach of courtesy -> to excuse oneself

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실례하다

실수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 실수 (失手), meaning 'mistake, blunder, slip, oversight', literally 'a slip of the hand (originally in baduk/chess or manual craft)', from 失 (실, 'miss, err, lose') + 手 (수, 'hand, move').

history.meaning: slip of the hand or faulty move

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실수

실수하다.etymology: Sino-Korean verb meaning 'to make a mistake, blunder, slip up', formed from 실수 (失手, 'mistake, slip') plus verbalizer -하다.

history.meaning: to make a slip or error

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 실수하다

싫어하다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to dislike, hate, be averse to', derived from the subjective adjective 싫다 ('to be displeasing, disliked', Middle Korean 슬다 / 싫다) plus the psychological verb-forming auxiliary -어하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싫어하다

심각하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 심각 (深刻, 'serious, grave, acute, severe', literally 'deeply carved/incisive', from 深 'deep' + 刻 'carve, engrave') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심각하다

심다.etymology: Native Korean regular verb meaning 'to plant (a tree, flower, or seed); to instill (an idea or hope)', descending from Middle Korean 심다 / 심그다 ('to plant').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심다

심심하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'bored, having nothing to do; slightly bland or undersalted in flavor', formed from the reduplicated root 심심- + -하다. Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 심심하다 (甚深-, 'profound, deep', used in formal expressions of gratitude or sympathy).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심심하다

심장.etymology: Sino-Korean anatomical compound 심장 (心臟), meaning 'the heart (organ)', composed of 心 (심, 'heart, mind') + 臟 (장, 'internal organ, viscera').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심장

심지어.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb 심지어 (甚至於), meaning 'even, going so far as to, to the extreme that', borrowed from the Classical Chinese connective phrase 甚至於 (甚 'extremely, even' + 至 'reach' + 於 'to, at').

history.meaning: reaching even to the point of
even, what is more, so much so that

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심지어

심하다.etymology: Sino-Korean adjective formed from 심 (甚, 'extreme, excessive, severe, intense') plus the adjective-forming suffix -하다 (Middle Korean 심ᄒᆞ다).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 심하다

십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 십 (十, Middle Chinese *dzyip*), meaning 'ten (10)'.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십

십사.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 십사 (十四), meaning 'fourteen (14)', formed from 十 (십, 'ten') + 四 (사, 'four').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십사

십오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 십오 (十五), meaning 'fifteen (15)', formed from 十 (십, 'ten') + 五 (오, 'five').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십오

십이.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 십이 (十二), meaning 'twelve (12)', formed from 十 (십, 'ten') + 二 (이, 'two').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 십이

싱싱하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'fresh, crisp, lively, full of vitality (of vegetables, fruit, fish, trees, or youth)', formed from the reduplicated expressive root 싱싱- plus -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싱싱하다

싶다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary adjective meaning 'to want to, wish to (after -고)' or 'to seem, feel like, wonder if (after clause endings)', descending from Middle Korean 식브다 / 십다 ('to feel inclined, seem').

history.meaning: to want to (-고 싶다); to think/seem that

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싶다

싸다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adjective uniting three Middle Korean words spelled ᄡᅡ다: (1) transitive verb 'to wrap, pack, bundle'; (2) adjective 'cheap, inexpensive' (which in Middle Korean meant 'to be worth its price' before shifting to 'low-priced, cheap'); and (3) verb 'to excrete, discharge'.

history.meaning: to wrap up; to be worth/cheap; to excrete

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싸다

싸인.etymology: Colloquial orthographic variant (reflecting the widespread tensified pronunciation [싸인]) of 사인, borrowed from English sign ('signature, autograph; signal or gesture').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 싸인

쌍둥이.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'twins', combining Sino-Korean 쌍 (雙, 'pair, couple, twin', Middle Korean 솽) with the native Korean person-forming suffix -둥이 ('child or person born with a given trait', Middle Korean 솽동이).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쌍둥이

쌓다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to pile up, stack, build up, accumulate (stones, snow, wealth, or experience)', descending from Middle Korean 샇다 ('to pile up, build') with initial glottalization (ㅅ > ㅆ).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쌓다

쌓이다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb meaning 'to be piled up, accumulate, build up', descending from Middle Korean 사히다 (derived from 샇다 > 쌓다 'to pile up' + passive suffix -이-).

history.meaning: to pile up, accumulate, be stacked

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쌓이다

썰다.etymology: Native Korean ㄹ-stem transitive verb meaning 'to slice, chop, dice, cut into pieces', descending from Middle Korean 섨다 / 썰다 ('to slice, chop').

history.meaning: to cut into slices or pieces

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 썰다

쏟다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to pour out, spill, empty out; to pour (one's heart, effort, or attention) into', descending from Middle Korean 쏫다 ('to pour out, spill').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쏟다

쏟아지다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb meaning 'to pour down (of heavy rain or sunlight), gush out, spill over, flood in (of questions or sleepiness)', formed from 쏟다 ('to pour out') plus the inchoative/passive auxiliary -아지다.

history.meaning: to be poured out, gush forth
to pour down, spill out, cascade

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쏟아지다

쓰다.etymology: Core native Korean 으-irregular verb and adjective uniting four Middle Korean words: (1) 쓰다 ('to write, compose'); (2) ᄡᅳ다 ('to use, employ, spend money'); (3) 쓰다 ('to wear on the head—a hat, glasses, mask—or hold overhead like an umbrella'); and (4) adjective ᄡᅳ다 ('bitter in taste').

history.form: 쓰다 (write; wear on head) / ᄡᅳ다 (use, spend; bitter)
history.meaning: to write; to wear on the head; to use; to be bitter
to write; to use/spend; to wear (hat/glasses); bitter

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쓰다

쓰레기통.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'trash can, wastebasket, garbage bin', combining native Korean 쓰레기 ('rubbish, trash, sweepings', derived from 쓸다 'to sweep' + nominal suffix -에기) with Sino-Korean 통 (桶, 'tub, bin, container').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 쓰레기통

씨.etymology: Polysemous Korean word representing two common lineages: (1) Sino-Korean bound honorific noun 씨 (氏, Middle Chinese *dzyeX*), used after a full or given name to mean 'Mr., Ms., -san' (or after a surname for 'clan, family'); and (2) native Korean noun 씨 ('seed, kernel, pit, stock/lineage'), descending from Middle Korean ᄡᅵ.

history.meaning: polite title, clan name (氏); seed, kernel (ᄡᅵ)

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 씨

씩씩하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'energetic, brave, spirited, vigorous, plucky', descending from Middle Korean 식식ᄒᆞ다 ('imposing, spirited, vigorous') via expressive initial tensification (ㅅ > ㅆ).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 씩씩하다

아.etymology: Primary native Korean vocalic interjection expressing sudden realization, recollection, surprise, or mild dismay ('ah!, oh!'), attested from Middle Korean texts onward.

history.meaning: exclamation of emotion, realization, or surprise

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아

아가씨.etymology: Native Korean noun meaning 'young lady, unmarried woman, miss', descending from Early Modern Korean 아기씨 / 아가씨, originally a respectful compound of 아기/아가 ('young daughter of a household') plus the honorific suffix -씨 (氏).

history.meaning: respected young unmarried daughter; young lady
young lady, miss; husband's younger sister

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아가씨

아까.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb meaning 'a little while ago, earlier (today), just now', descending from Middle Korean 아까 / 악가.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아까

아끼다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb meaning 'to cherish, treasure, value dearly; to save, use sparingly, begrudge spending', descending from Middle Korean 앗기다 ('to spare, begrudge, hold dear') via assimilation/glottalization (ㅅㄱ > ㄲ).

history.meaning: to cherish, treasure; to save, economize on

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아끼다

아늑하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective meaning 'cozy, snug, sheltered, quietly warm and comfortable', formed from the light-vowel expressive root 아늑- (counterpart of 어늑-) plus -하다.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아늑하다

아니다.etymology: Core native Korean negative copula (classified in Korean grammar as an adjective) meaning 'not to be, be not', descending from Middle Korean 아니다, formed by fusing the negative noun/adverb 아니 ('not') with the copula -이다 ('to be').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아니다

아니면.etymology: Native Korean conjunction and adverb meaning 'or, otherwise, if not', grammaticalized from the conditional form of the negative copula 아니다 (stem 아니- + conditional connective ending -면, literally 'if it is not').

history.meaning: if it is not -> otherwise, or

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아니면

아니요.etymology: Polite native Korean negative response interjection meaning 'no', formed from the negative root 아니 ('no, not') plus the polite addressee particle -요.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아니요

아래.etymology: Core native Korean locative noun meaning 'bottom, lower part, underneath, below', descending from Middle Korean 아래, originally a fossilized locative form combining the archaic noun 알 ('bottom, underside') with the locative particle -애 ('at, in').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아래

아래쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun meaning 'lower side, bottom part, downward direction', formed from 아래 ('bottom, below') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아래쪽

아래층.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'lower floor, downstairs', combining native Korean 아래 ('below, lower part') with Sino-Korean 층 (層, 'floor, story, level').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아래층

아름답다.etymology: Native Korean ㅂ-irregular adjective meaning 'beautiful, lovely, admirable', descending from Middle Korean 아ᄅᆞᆷ답다, formed from the Middle Korean noun 아ᄅᆞᆷ ('one's own self/character, worth, beauty', related to 알다 'to know/understand') plus the adjective-forming suffix -답다 ('having the true quality of').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아름답다

아마.etymology: Native Korean epistemic modal adverb meaning 'probably, perhaps, maybe, likely', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 아마.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아마

아몬드.etymology: Borrowed from English almond ('edible oval nut/seed of the almond tree, Prunus amygdalus').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아몬드

아무.etymology: Native Korean indefinite pronoun and determiner meaning 'any, anyone, anybody (typically used with negative or concessive predicates)', descending from Middle Korean 아모 ('anyone, any').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아무

아무것.etymology: Native Korean compound indefinite pronoun meaning 'anything (or, with negative predicates, nothing at all)', formed from the determiner 아무 ('any', Middle Korean 아모) + bound noun 것 ('thing').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아무것

아쉽게도.etymology: Native Korean sentence adverb meaning 'unfortunately, regrettably, to one's regret', derived from the adjective 아쉽다 ('regrettable, leaving something to be desired, sorry to part', Middle Korean 아싀엽다) + adverbial ending -게 + particle -도 ('even/indeed').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아쉽게도

아야.etymology: Native Korean interjection expressing sudden sharp physical pain ('ouch!, ow!'), attested since Early Modern Korean.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아야

아예.etymology: Native Korean adverb meaning 'from the very beginning, altogether, completely, at all (especially with negative or resolute statements)', descending from Early Modern Korean 아예 / 아이에.

history.meaning: from the start, altogether, at all

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아예

아이.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'child, kid, youngster', descending from Middle Korean 아히 ('child') via loss of intervocalic ㅎ (아히 > 아이). Also used as an exclamation of mild dismay or surprise.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이

아이고.etymology: Classic native Korean interjection expressing pain, grief, exhaustion, surprise, or relief ('oh my!, alas!, dear me!, whew!'), attested from Middle Korean 아이고 onward.

history.meaning: exclamation of grief, pain, or surprise

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이고

아이구.etymology: Expressive variant of the native Korean interjection 아이고 ('oh my!, goodness!, whew!'), formed by raising the final vowel (오 > 우) for a softer or more colloquial nuance.

history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, relief, or ache

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이구

아이쿠.etymology: Native Korean interjection uttered when suddenly startled, stumbling, dropping something, or realizing a mistake ('whoops!, oops!, oh dear!'), formed as an aspirated expressive variant of 아이구/아이고.

history.meaning: aspirated exclamation of sudden startle or slip

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아이쿠

아저씨.etymology: Native Korean kinship and social noun meaning 'uncle (parent's brother or aunt's husband); middle-aged man, mister', descending from Middle Korean 아자비 ('uncle') reshaped in Early Modern Korean with the honorific suffix -씨 (아자비 + -씨 > 아저씨).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아저씨

아주.etymology: Native Korean degree adverb meaning 'very, extremely; completely, for good', descending from Middle Korean 아조 ('completely, altogether, very') via vowel raising (오 > 우).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아주

아직.etymology: Native Korean temporal adverb meaning 'still, yet', descending from Middle Korean 아짇 / 아직 ('still, while yet').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아직

아치.etymology: Borrowed from English arch ('curved masonry or structural opening spanning a doorway, bridge, or passage'), ultimately from Latin arcus ('bow, arch').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아치

아치문.etymology: Hybrid compound noun meaning 'arched doorway, archway, arch gate', combining the English loanword 아치 (arch) with Sino-Korean 문 (門, 'door, gate').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아치문

아침.etymology: Core native Korean noun meaning 'morning; breakfast (morning meal)', descending from Middle Korean 아ᄎᆞᆷ ('morning; breakfast') via vowel fronting/raising (ᆞ > ㅣ after ㅊ).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아침

아프다.etymology: Native Korean 으-irregular adjective meaning 'painful, sore, aching, sick, hurt', descending from Middle Korean 알프다 ('painful, aching'), derived from the verb stem 앓- (앓다, 'to suffer from illness or pain') plus the adjective-forming suffix -브다 (> -프다).

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아프다

아하.etymology: Native Korean interjection expressing sudden comprehension, discovery, or realization ('aha!, I see!'), formed from 아 ('ah') + 하 ('ha').

history.meaning: exclamation of sudden realization or understanding

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아하

아홉.etymology: Core native Korean numeral meaning 'nine (9)', attested unchanged in form since Middle Korean 아홉.

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 아홉

악보.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 악보 (樂譜), meaning 'sheet music, musical score', composed of 樂 (악, 'music') + 譜 (보, 'score, chart, register').

history.meaning: written notation or score of music

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 악보

악절.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 악절 (樂節), meaning 'musical phrase, period, or passage in a composition', composed of 樂 (악, 'music') + 節 (절, 'section, joint, phrase, measure').

history.meaning: structural section or phrase of a musical piece

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 악절

안.etymology: Core native Korean word representing two everyday lineages: (1) noun 안 ('inside, interior, within'), descending from Middle Korean 안ㅎ (an ㅎ-final noun, which is why 안 + 밖 'outside' yields 안팎 'inside and outside'); and (2) negative adverb 안 ('not'), contracted from 아니 (Middle Korean 아니). Also homophonous with Sino-Korean 안 (案, 'plan, proposal, draft').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 안

안경.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안경 (眼鏡), literally 'eye-mirror/lens', from 안 (眼, 'eye') + 경 (鏡, 'mirror, lens').
안경.notes: Takes the verb 쓰다 ('안경을 쓰다') when putting glasses on.

안내문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안내문 (案內文), meaning 'information notice, guide text, written announcement', formed from 안내 (案內, 'guidance, showing the way, information') + 문 (文, 'writing, text, notice').

history.meaning: written text providing guidance or information

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 안내문

안내판.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안내판 (案內板), meaning 'information board, signboard, directory sign', formed from 안내 (案內, 'guidance, information') + 판 (板, 'board, plaque, sign').

sources.title: NIKL Standard Korean Language Dictionary — 안내판

안녕.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being'), joining 안 (安, 'peaceful, safe') and 녕 (寧, 'tranquil, at ease'); used in Modern Korean as an informal greeting ('hello; goodbye').

안녕하세요.etymology: Built from Sino-Korean 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being'), the adjective-forming verb 하다, and the polite honorific ending -세요 (contracted from -시어요). Literally asks or wishes 'Are you at peace?'.
안녕하세요.notes: Used across South Korea at any hour of the day as the standard polite greeting.

안녕히.etymology: Hybrid Korean adverb formed from Sino-Korean 안녕 (安寧, 'peace and well-being') + native Korean adverbial suffix -히 ('in a ... manner'), used in polite greetings and farewells such as 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

안마당.etymology: Native Korean compound combining 안 ('inside, inner') with 마당 ('courtyard, yard').
안마당.notes: Traditional Korean courtyard houses arrange rooms around a sheltered 안마당 open to the sky.

안심.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안심 (安心), joining 안 (安, 'peaceful, calm') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind') — literally 'setting one's mind at rest'; also has a homonymous native culinary sense ('tenderloin, inner fillet of meat', from 안 'inside' + 힘/심 'sinew, muscle').

history.meaning: putting the mind at ease, relief
peace of mind, relief; inner tenderloin cut

안전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 안전 (安全), joining 안 (安, 'peaceful, secure') and 전 (全, 'whole, intact, complete') — literally 'safe and intact'.

history.meaning: free from danger, intact and secure

안전하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 안전 (安全, 'safety, security') + native light verb/adjective-forming suffix -하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: to be safe, free from danger

안쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 안 ('inside, interior', Middle Korean 안ㅎ) + 쪽 ('side, direction').

앉다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 앉다 ('to sit, take a seat').

않다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary negation verb/adjective, contracted from 아니하다 ('not to do, not to be'), itself from negative adverb 아니 ('not') + 하다 ('to do, be').

알다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 알다 ('to know, understand, recognize').

history.meaning: to know, understand, be aware of

알람.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed in the 20th century from English alarm (ultimately from Italian all'arme! 'to arms!').

history.meaning: wake-up alarm clock or warning signal

알리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 알외다 / 알리다, formed from 알다 ('to know') + causative suffix -리- ('to cause to know').

history.meaning: to make known, inform, notify, announce

알아보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 알다 ('to know, recognize', conjunctive form 알아) + auxiliary/exploratory verb 보다 ('to see, try').

history.meaning: to recognize; to inquire into, check out, investigate

압력.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 압력 (壓力), joining 압 (壓, 'to press down, crush') and 력 (力, 'force, power, strength').

history.meaning: pressing force, physical or social pressure

앞.etymology: Native Korean spatial noun descending from Middle Korean 앞 ('front, forepart; presence').

앞당겨지다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 앞당기다 ('to pull forward, move a date/time earlier', from 앞 'front' + 당기다 'to pull') + passive auxiliary -어지다.

history.meaning: to be moved forward or brought earlier in schedule

앞자리.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 앞 ('front') + 자리 ('seat, place, position, digit place').

history.meaning: front seat; leading digit of a number

앞장서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 앞장 ('the very head or vanguard of a group', from 앞 'front' + 장) + 서다 ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand at the head, take the lead, walk in front

앞쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 앞 ('front') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

약국.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 약국 (藥局), joining 약 (藥, 'medicine, medicinal herb, drug') and 국 (局, 'office, bureau, shop, dispensary').

약속.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 약속 (約束), combining 약 (約, 'bind, agree') and 속 (束, 'tie, bundle').
약속.notes: Covers both a personal promise ('약속해요!') and a scheduled appointment or plan with someone.

약속하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 약속 (約束, 'promise, appointment, pact', from 約 'to bind, make a covenant' + 束 'to tie in a bundle, restrain') + native verb-forming suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to make a promise or appointment

약하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 약 (弱, 'weak, fragile, slender') + native adjective-forming suffix -하다.

얇다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 얣겁다 / 엷다 (bright-vowel variant 얇다, 'to be thin, not thick, of flat objects').

history.meaning: to be thin, slender in thickness
to be thin (of paper, cloth, ice, slices)

양동이.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound formed in the late 19th–early 20th century from Sino-Korean prefix 양- (洋-, 'Western, foreign, across the ocean') + native Korean 동이 ('large round earthenware water jar') — literally 'Western-style metal bucket'.

양모.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 양모 (羊毛), from 양 (羊, 'sheep') and 모 (毛, 'hair, wool, fur').
양모.notes: Dense compressed 양모 forms the felt hammers inside acoustic pianos.

양쪽.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 양 (兩, 'both, pair, two') + native Korean 쪽 ('side, direction').

얘.etymology: Contracted colloquial Korean noun and interjection from 이 아이 ('this child, this kid'), used to call a child or close younger friend ('hey, listen') or refer to 'this person/kid'.

어.etymology: Natural native Korean exclamation uttered when suddenly noticing something, hesitating, or expressing mild surprise ('oh, uh, hey').

history.meaning: interjection of sudden realization, surprise, or informal affirmation

어깨.etymology: Native Korean anatomical noun descending from Middle Korean 어께 ('shoulder').

어느.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite determiner descending from Middle Korean 어느 ('which, what, some').

어둡다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 어듭다 ('to be dark, dim, gloomy').

history.meaning: to be dark, dim, poorly informed about

어디.etymology: Native Korean interrogative and indefinite place pronoun descending from Middle Korean 어드메 / 어디 ('where, what place, somewhere').

어디에나.etymology: Native Korean adverbial phrase formed from 어디 ('where, any place') + locative particle -에 ('at, in') + inclusive particle -나 ('or, regardless of, every').
