어떡하다.etymology: Phonological contraction in spoken and standard Korean of 어떠하게 하다 / 어떻게 하다 ('to do how, what to do about something').

history.meaning: to do what, how to handle a situation

어떤.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner contracted from 어떠하- (어떻다, 'to be of what kind') + adnominal suffix -ㄴ.

history.meaning: what kind of, which; some, a certain

어떻게.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 어떠하게, adverbial form (-게) of 어떠하다 / 어떻다 ('to be how, be in what state').

어떻다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb contracted from 어떠하다 (Middle Korean 어떠하다, 'to be how, be of what sort or state').

history.meaning: to be in what state or manner
to be how, be like what

어리다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 어리다; famously meant 'to be foolish, naive, simple-minded' in 15th-century Middle Korean (as in the opening preface of the Hunminjeongeum, 어린 백성 'unlettered/simple common folk') before shifting to 'to be young in age, tender'.

history.meaning: to be young in years, juvenile

어머.etymology: Native Korean exclamation of surprise or mild dismay, originating as a shortened vocative of 어머니 / 엄마 ('mother!, oh my!').

어머나.etymology: Native Korean interjection of surprise formed from 어머 ('oh my!') + expressive exclamatory particle -나.

어머니.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun descending from Middle Korean 어마님 / 어미 ('mother', built on the ancient maternal root 엄-/어마 plus honorific suffix -니).

어서.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 어서 ('quickly, promptly, without delay; welcomingly').

어울리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 어울다 / 어우르다 ('to join together, mingle, match harmoniously'), derived from the passive/causative stem 어울리-.

history.meaning: to suit, match well, look good on; to socialize with

어제.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 어제 ('yesterday').

어젯밤.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 어제 ('yesterday') + genitive/compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 밤 ('night').

어쩌다.etymology: Native Korean verb and adverb contracted from 어찌하다 ('to do how, do what'); as an adverb (short for 어쩌다가), means 'by chance, accidentally, once in a while'.

history.meaning: to do what; by chance, unintentionally, occasionally

어쩐지.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 어찌한지 ('for what reason it may be, somehow'), from 어찌하다 + indirect question ending -ㄴ지.

history.meaning: somehow, for some reason; no wonder!

언니.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun (attested from Early Modern Korean 언니) used by a female speaker to address or refer to an older sister (and formerly also used between males for an elder brother in Seoul speech), extended to friendly older female acquaintances.

history.meaning: older sister (of a female); friendly address to an older woman

언덕.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 언덕 ('hill, bank, slope, rising ground').

얼굴.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 얼굴; originally meant 'overall bodily shape, figure, form, appearance' in 15th-century Middle Korean (while 낯 meant 'face'), before narrowing in Early Modern Korean to 'human face, countenance'.

history.meaning: bodily shape, overall figure or form

얼룩.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 어루기 / 얼룩 ('mottled pattern, spot, dapple, stain').

얼른.etymology: Native Korean mimetic/expressive adverb meaning 'in a flash, quickly, right away, without hesitation'.

얼마나.etymology: Native Korean adverb formed from 얼마 ('how much, how many, what quantity', from Middle Korean 언마) + emphatic particle -나.

history.meaning: how much, to what degree, how very!

얼음.etymology: Native Korean deverbal noun formed from 얼다 ('to freeze') + nominalizing suffix -음.
얼음.notes: Retains morphophonemic spelling 얼음 (pronounced [어름]) showing its derivation from 얼-.

얼음물.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 얼음 ('ice', nominalization in -음 of 얼다 'to freeze') + 물 ('water').

얼음장.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 얼음 ('ice') + Sino-Korean/classifier 장 (張/場, 'flat sheet or slab') — literally 'a thick sheet or slab of ice'.

history.meaning: sheet or cake of ice; something icy cold

엄마.etymology: Native Korean affectionate/informal kinship noun ('mom, mommy'), descending from the nursery and vocative root 어마 (cf. Middle Korean 어미 / 어마님).

없다.etymology: Native Korean existential negation adjective descending from Middle Korean 없다 ('not to exist, be lacking, not to have').

history.meaning: to not be, not exist, not have

없이.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 업시, formed from the stem 없- (없다, 'not to exist, lack') + adverbial suffix -이.

에.etymology: Native Korean locative/dative/allative case particle descending from Middle Korean 애 / 에 / 예 (which harmonized with the preceding vowel), marking static location ('in, at, on'), time ('at'), or destination ('to').

에서.etymology: Native Korean ablative and dynamic-locative case particle descending from Middle Korean 애셔 / 에셔, grammaticalized from locative particle 에 + 서 (converbal form 시어 of 이시다 / 있다 'to be, exist' — literally 'being at [a place], from').

history.meaning: being at -> at (place of action); from (point of departure)
at, in (where an action happens); from

엔진.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed in the 20th century from English engine (ultimately from Latin ingenium 'innate talent, clever contrivance').

여기.etymology: Native Korean proximal place pronoun descending from Middle Korean 예 / 여기 ('this place, here', built on proximal demonstrative root 이-/여- + place suffix -기).

여덟.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 여듧 ('eight').

여러분.etymology: Native Korean honorific second-person plural pronoun formed from 여러 ('many, several, various', Middle Korean 여러) + honorific person classifier 분 ('esteemed person').

history.meaning: everyone, ladies and gentlemen, all of you

여름.etymology: Native Korean seasonal noun descending from Middle Korean 녀름 ('summer'); in 15th-century Middle Korean, 녀름 also meant 'fruits of the earth, harvest, farming' (derived from 녈- / 열다 'to bear fruit'), because summer is the growing season.

여보세요.etymology: Native Korean attention-getting interjection and standard telephone greeting, contracted from 여기 보셔요 / 여기 보세요 ('look here, excuse me', from 여기 'here' + 보시다 'to look [honorific]').

history.meaning: look here!, excuse me!; hello? (on the telephone)

여분.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 여분 (餘分), joining 여 (餘, 'surplus, remainder, left over') and 분 (分, 'share, portion, part').

여섯.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 여슷 ('six').

여성분.etymology: Polite compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 여성 (女性, 'woman, female gender', from 女 'woman' + 性 'sex, nature') + native Korean honorific person classifier 분 ('esteemed person').

여유롭다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 여유 (餘裕, 'surplus, room to spare, composure', from 餘 'surplus' + 裕 'abundant, unhurried') + native adjectival suffix -롭다 ('characterized by').

history.meaning: to be unhurried, relaxed, composed, having plenty to spare

여행.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 여행 (旅行), joining 여 (旅, 'travel, journey, troop') and 행 (行, 'to go, walk, travel').

history.meaning: going on a journey, travel, trip

여행책.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun formed from 여행 (旅行, 'travel, trip') + 책 (冊, 'book, volume').

역.etymology: Sino-Korean morpheme 역 (驛, originally 'mounted post-horse relay station' in premodern East Asia, adapted in the late 19th century for a railway or subway 'station'; also 役 'role, part, service' or 域 'area, zone').

연결되다.etymology: Hybrid passive verb formed from Sino-Korean 연결 (連結, 'connection, linking', from 連 'to link, join continuously' + 結 'to tie, bind') + native passive/inchoative verb 되다 ('to become, be made').

history.meaning: to be connected, linked, joined together

연구하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 연구 (硏究, 'research, deep study', from 硏 'to grind, polish, rub fine' + 究 'to examine thoroughly, probe to the bottom') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to research, study in depth, investigate

연락.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연락 (連絡 / 聯絡), joining 연 (連/聯, 'to link, join in a row') and 락 (絡, 'thread, network, connect').

history.meaning: connection, keeping in touch, communication, contact

연설문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연설문 (演說文), joining 연설 (演說, 'public speech, address', from 演 'to expound, perform' + 說 'to speak, explain') and 문 (文, 'writing, text').

history.meaning: written text or script of a public speech

연습하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 연습 (練習, 'practice, drill, rehearsal', from 練 'to boil and bleach raw silk, train, drill' + 習 'to flap wings repeatedly, practice') + native verb suffix -하다.

연주.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연주 (演奏), joining 연 (演, 'to perform, unfold, practice') and 주 (奏, 'to play music, present to a ruler').

연필.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 연필 (鉛筆), joining 연 (鉛, 'lead metal') and 필 (筆, 'writing brush, pen') — literally 'lead brush' (historically used in China for lead styluses, and adapted in the late 19th century as a calque of European 'lead pencil').

열.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 열 ('ten', pre-noun form 열); also homonymous with Sino-Korean 열 (熱, 'heat, fever, enthusiasm') and 열 (列, 'row, line').

열기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 열기 (熱氣), joining 열 (熱, 'heat, hot') and 기 (氣, 'air, vapor, energy, atmosphere').

history.meaning: hot air, heat; heated enthusiasm or excitement

열다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 열다 ('to open a door, lid, or passage; to unlock, begin').

열두.etymology: Native Korean pre-nominal compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 두 (adnominal form of 둘 'two', Middle Korean 열둘).

열리다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb descending from Middle Korean 열이다, formed from 열다 ('to open') + passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to be opened, open by itself, be held (of a meeting or market)

열쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound built from the prospective stem 열- of 열다 ('to open') and 쇠 ('iron, metal'): literally 'opening-metal'.
열쇠.notes: Pairs naturally with 잠그다 ('to lock') and 열다 ('to open').

열아홉.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 아홉 ('nine', Middle Korean 아홉).

열여섯.etymology: Native Korean compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 여섯 ('six', Middle Korean 여슷), pronounced [열려섣] with [n]-insertion and liquidization.

열한.etymology: Native Korean pre-nominal compound numeral formed from 열 ('ten') + 한 (adnominal form of 하나 'one', Middle Korean 열하나).

엽서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 엽서 (葉書), joining 엽 (葉, 'leaf, thin flat sheet') and 서 (書, 'letter, writing') — literally 'leaf-letter', coined in Meiji Japan (hagaki) and adopted into Korean for a postal card.

엿보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 엿보다 ('to peep, spy on, watch for an opportunity'), from verb stem 엿- ('to lurk, watch stealthily') + 보다 ('to look, see').

history.meaning: to peep through a crack, spy on, watch for a chance

영미.etymology: Korean female given name 영미 (commonly written in Hanja as 英美, combining 英 'flower petal, outstanding, brilliant' and 美 'beautiful', or 永美 'eternal beauty').

영수증.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 영수증 (領受證), joining 영수 (領受, 'receiving and taking into possession', from 領 'to lead, receive' + 受 'to receive') and 증 (證, 'certificate, proof, voucher').

history.meaning: written proof of payment received, receipt

영업하다.etymology: Sino-Korean 영업 (營業, 영 'manage, run' + 업 'business, trade') + -하다.
영업하다.notes: Standard term on Korean shopfront signs (영업중 'Open', 매일 영업합니다 'Open Daily').

영웅.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 영웅 (英雄), joining 영 (英, 'outstanding blossom, person of exceptional talent') and 웅 (雄, 'male bird, vigorous leader, champion').

history.meaning: person of extraordinary valor and ability, hero

옆.etymology: Native Korean spatial noun descending from Middle Korean 옆 ('side, flank of the body, space beside').

옆구리.etymology: Native Korean anatomical compound descending from Middle Korean 옆구리, formed from 옆 ('side') + 구리 (bound root denoting a curved flank or hollow of the torso).

history.meaning: side of the torso between ribs and hip, flank

옆면.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 옆 ('side') + Sino-Korean 면 (面, 'face, surface, side').

예쁘다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 어엿브다; in 15th-century Middle Korean (famously in the Hunminjeongeum preface, 내 이를 위하야 어엿비 너겨 'I, feeling pity for them on this account'), 어엿브다 meant 'pitiful, touching, arousing tender compassion', which shifted in Early Modern Korean to 'endearing, lovely, pretty'.

예산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 예산 (豫算), combining 예 (豫, 'beforehand, in advance') and 산 (算, 'count, calculate').
예산.notes: Shares the calculation root 산 (算) with 계산 ('payment / calculation').

예약.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 예약 (豫約), from 예 (豫, 'beforehand, in advance') and 약 (約, 'agreement, booking').
예약.notes: Standard noun for hotel, restaurant, and train reservations; pairs with 하다 ('예약하다').

예약하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 예약 (豫約, 'advance booking or pledge', from 豫 'beforehand, in advance' + 約 'agreement, promise') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to book in advance, make a reservation

예전.etymology: Hybrid temporal noun formed from native Korean 예 ('olden times, the past', Middle Korean 녜) + Sino-Korean 전 (前, 'before, former times').

history.meaning: former times, the old days, before

옛.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner descending from Middle Korean 녯, formed from 녜 ('olden times, antiquity') + genitive particle -ㅅ.

옛날.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 녯날, formed from 녯 / 옛 ('of old') + 날 ('day, time').

history.meaning: olden days, long ago, once upon a time

오.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 오 (五, 'five'), from Middle Chinese *nguX; also used as a natural Korean exclamation 오 ('oh!, ah!').

오늘.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun descending from Middle Korean 오늘 ('today', analyzed historically as proximal deictic root 오- 'this' + 날/늘 'day').

오다.etymology: Native Korean basic motion verb descending from Middle Korean 오다 ('to come, move toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to come, arrive; (of rain or snow) to fall

오래다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb formed from the adverb/noun root 오래 ('a long time', Middle Korean 오라다 'to be long in time').

history.meaning: to be of long standing, take a long time

오래되다.etymology: Native Korean compound descriptive/intransitive verb formed from 오래 ('for a long time') + 되다 ('to become, pass, elapse').

history.meaning: to be old, date back a long time

오렌지.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English orange (ultimately via Old French, Italian, Arabic, and Persian from Sanskrit naranga).

오른쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 오른 (adnominal form of 옳다 'to be right, proper, straight', Middle Korean 옳-) + 쪽 ('side, direction') — just like English 'right' and French 'droit', linking moral/practical 'rightness' with the right-hand side.

오만.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 오만 (五萬, 'fifty thousand', joining 五 'five' + 萬 'ten thousand'); homonymous with Sino-Korean 오만 (傲慢, 'arrogance, haughtiness').

오븐.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English oven (from Old English ofen 'furnace, baking chamber').

오성급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 오성급 (五星級), joining 오 (五, 'five'), 성 (星, 'star'), and 급 (級, 'grade, class, rank') — a calque of international 'five-star rating'.

history.meaning: five-star class or rating (especially of a hotel)

오십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 오십 (五十), joining 오 (五, 'five') and 십 (十, 'ten').

오월.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 오월 (五月), joining 오 (五, 'five') and 월 (月, 'month, moon') — literally 'fifth month'.

오후.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 오후 (午後), joining 오 (午, 'noon, seventh Earthly Branch 11 a.m.–1 p.m.') and 후 (後, 'after, behind') — literally 'after noon'.

옥타브.etymology: Modern musical loanword borrowed from English octave or French octave (ultimately from Latin octava 'eighth').

history.meaning: musical octave (interval of eight diatonic degrees)

온기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 온기 (溫氣), joining 온 (溫, 'warm, gentle') and 기 (氣, 'air, breath, energy').
온기.notes: Shares 온 (溫) with 온실 ('conservatory / greenhouse', 溫室).

온수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 온수 (溫水), joining 온 (溫, 'warm, lukewarm') and 수 (水, 'water').

history.meaning: warm or hot water (for bathing or washing)

온실.notes: Used for plant greenhouses and for glass sunrooms; the same 室 'room' appears in 사무실 'office' and 지하실 'basement'.

올라가다.etymology: Native Korean directional compound verb descending from Middle Korean 올아가다, formed from 오르다 ('to rise, climb, ascend', conjunctive 올라) + deictic motion verb 가다 ('to go away from the speaker').

history.meaning: to go up, climb, ascend, rise (in price or temperature)

올라오다.etymology: Native Korean directional compound verb descending from Middle Korean 올아오다, formed from 오르다 ('to rise, ascend', conjunctive 올라) + deictic motion verb 오다 ('to come toward the speaker').

history.meaning: to come up, climb up toward here

올려다보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 올리다 ('to raise, lift up', conjunctive 올려) + directive particle -다 + 보다 ('to look at').

history.meaning: to look up at, gaze upward

올리다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 올이다, formed from 오르다 ('to go up, rise') + causative suffix -리- ('to cause to rise, raise').

history.meaning: to raise, lift up, place on top, offer respectfully, post online

올리브유.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining the English loanword 올리브 (olive) + Sino-Korean 유 (油, 'oil').

옮기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 옮기다, formed from 옮다 ('to move from one place to another, shift, spread') + causative suffix -기-.

history.meaning: to move something to another place, transfer, translate

완벽하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 완벽 (完璧, 'flawlessness, perfection', from a classical Chinese historical idiom 完璧歸趙 meaning 'to return the priceless Heshibi jade disc whole and unscathed [完] to the State of Zhao') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.form: 完璧 ('unscathed jade disc') -> 완벽 + -하다 -> 완벽하다

완성되다.etymology: Hybrid passive/inchoative verb formed from Sino-Korean 완성 (完成, 'completion, perfection', from 完 'whole, complete' + 成 'to accomplish, achieve') + native 되다 ('to become, be made').

history.meaning: to be completed, finished, brought to perfection

완성하다.etymology: Hybrid transitive verb formed from Sino-Korean 완성 (完成, 'completion', from 完 'complete' + 成 'accomplish') + native verb suffix -하다.

완전히.etymology: Hybrid adverb formed from Sino-Korean 완전 (完全, 'completeness, wholeness', from 完 'whole' + 全 'intact, entire') + native adverbial suffix -히.

완충재.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 완충재 (緩衝材), joining 완충 (緩衝, 'buffering, softening a shock', from 緩 'slack, gentle, slow' + 衝 'collision, impact') and 재 (材, 'material, timber').

history.meaning: shock-absorbing packing material, cushioning (such as bubble wrap or styrofoam)

왈츠.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed via English waltz from German Walzer ('triple-time ballroom dance', derived from walzen 'to revolve, roll, glide').

history.meaning: waltz dance or music in 3/4 time

왜.etymology: Native Korean interrogative adverb ('why, for what reason'), contracted in Early Modern Korean from Middle Korean 오🆈 / 어이 ('how, why').

외우다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 외오다 ('to recite from memory, learn by heart').

history.meaning: to memorize, learn by heart, recite

왼손.etymology: Native Korean compound of adnominal prefix 왼- ('left') and 손 ('hand').
왼손.notes: Pairs with 오른손 ('right hand') and 왼쪽 ('left side').

왼쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 왼 ('left-hand; originally twisted, reversed, wrong way', adnominal of Middle Korean 외다 'to be wrong, reversed') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

요리.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 요리 (料理), joining 료/요 (料, 'to measure grain, calculate, ingredients, material') and 리 (理, 'to dress jade, put in order, manage'); originally meant 'arranging and managing affairs', then specialized in East Asian usage to 'preparing food, cooking, dish'.

history.meaning: measuring and managing -> culinary preparation, cooking, dish

욕실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 욕실 (浴室), joining 욕 (浴, 'to bathe, wash the body') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

욕심내다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 욕심 (慾心, 'greed, covetousness, strong desire', from 慾 'desire, appetite' + 心 'heart, mind') + native Korean 내다 ('to put forth, produce, show').

history.meaning: to show greed, covet, be ambitious for more

우렁차다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb formed from the mimetic root 우렁- (evoking a deep, booming, resonant sound, as in 우렁우렁) + adjective-forming root 차다 ('to be full of').

history.meaning: to be booming, sonorous, loud and resonant

우리.etymology: Native Korean first-person plural pronoun descending from Middle Korean 우리 ('we, us, our', related to 울 / 우리 'enclosure, fence, fold, group sharing one enclosure').

history.meaning: we, us, our (often used for shared family, home, or country)

우산.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우산 (雨傘), joining 우 (雨, 'rain') and 산 (傘, 'umbrella, parasol').

우선.etymology: Sino-Korean compound adverb 우선 (于先 / 優先), joining 우 (于 'at, in' or 優 'surpassing, priority') and 선 (先, 'first, before, ahead').

history.meaning: first of all, before anything else, for now

우와.etymology: Natural Korean expressive interjection (variant of 와) voicing sudden amazement, admiration, or awe ('wow!, whoa!').

우유.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우유 (牛乳), joining 우 (牛, 'cow, cattle') and 유 (乳, 'breast, milk').

우체부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우체부 (郵遞夫), joining 우 (郵, 'post station, mail'), 체 (遞, 'to hand over in relay, deliver'), and 부 (夫, 'working man, carrier').

우편.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 우편 (郵便), joining 우 (郵, 'posthouse, mail relay') and 편 (便, 'convenience, dispatch, message, opportunity') — adopted in late 19th-century East Asian postal reforms for the modern postal service.

운.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 운 (運, 'revolving movement of heaven and earth, fate, fortune, luck'; also 韻 'rhyme, resonance').

울다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 울다 ('to cry, weep; of birds, beasts, wind, or bells, to call out, sing, ring').

history.meaning: to weep, cry; (of animals or bells) to sound

울리다.etymology: Native Korean causative/intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 울이다, formed from 울다 ('to cry, sound, ring') + suffix -리- ('to make cry; to cause to ring, resound, echo').

history.meaning: to make someone cry; to ring, echo, reverberate

울림.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun formed from 울리다 ('to ring, resound, reverberate') + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

움직이다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 움즈기다 ('to move, stir, shift'), formed on the mimetic root 움즉- ('stirring, budging slightly') + verbalizer -이다.

웃다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 웃다 (stem 웃-, 'to laugh, smile').

원.etymology: Sino-Korean morpheme 원: as the Korean currency unit ('won'), derived from 圓 ('round, round silver coin', cognate with Chinese yuan and Japanese yen); also represents 願 ('wish, desire') or 院 ('courtyard building, institute').

history.meaning: round coin -> base unit of Korean currency (KRW)

원래.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 원래 (原來), joining 원 (原, 'source, origin, high plain') and 래 (來, 'coming from, since') — literally 'coming from the origin'.

history.meaning: from the very beginning, originally, by nature

원피스.etymology: 20th-century loanword from English one-piece (short for one-piece dress), designating a woman's dress in which bodice and skirt form a single garment.

원하다.etymology: Hybrid transitive verb formed from Sino-Korean 원 (願, 'wish, desire, vow') + native verb suffix -하다.

월요일.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 월요일 (月曜日), joining 월 (月, 'Moon'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day') — literally 'Day of the Moon' (matching Latin dies Lunae).

위.etymology: Native Korean spatial noun descending from Middle Korean 우ㅎ ('top, upper part, above', which acquired the vowel -ㅣ from locative 우희 > 위에).

위쪽.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 위 ('top, above') + 쪽 ('side, direction').

history.meaning: the upper side, upward direction, top part

위층.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 위 ('top, upper') + Sino-Korean 층 (層, 'story, floor, layer').

위하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 위 (爲, 'to act for the sake of, serve, benefit') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to do for the sake of, care for, honor

윗줄.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 위 ('top, upper') + compound interfix -ㅅ- (사이시옷) + 줄 ('line, row, string').

유리.etymology: Sino-Korean 琉璃, borrowed from Chinese 琉璃 'glass, glaze'.
유리.notes: Found in 유리창 'glass window' and 유리컵 'drinking glass'.

유리방.etymology: Sino-Korean/hybrid compound noun formed from 유리 (琉璃, 'glass') + 방 (房, 'room, chamber').

유리병.etymology: Compound of 유리 (琉璃, an ancient Buddhist Sanskrit loanword via Classical Chinese meaning 'lapis / glass') and 병 (瓶, 'bottle, jar').
유리병.notes: Used in everyday Korean for both narrow-necked glass bottles and wide-mouthed honey or jam jars.

유리창.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 유리창 (琉璃窓), joining 유리 (琉璃, 'lapis lazuli, colored glaze, glass', itself an ancient Chinese transcription via Prakrit veluriya of Sanskrit vaidurya 'beryl, cat's-eye gem') and 창 (窓, 'window').

유리컵.etymology: Hybrid compound noun combining Sino-Korean 유리 (琉璃, 'glass') + English loanword 컵 (cup).

육.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 육 (六, 'six', initial form of 륙 before pause or vowel), from Middle Chinese *ljuwk.

육호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 육호실 (六號室), joining 육 (六, 'six'), 호 (號, 'number, designation'), and 실 (室, 'room').

으으.etymology: Natural Korean vocalic interjection expressing a shiver from cold, a groan of pain or effort, or revulsion ('brrr!, ugh!').

history.meaning: groan or shiver of cold, pain, or disgust

은.etymology: Native Korean topic/contrastive marker attached to consonant-final nouns (allomorph of 는 after vowels), descending from Middle Korean 은 / 으란; also homonymous with Sino-Korean noun 은 (銀, 'silver').

history.meaning: topic and contrast particle after consonants; also 銀 ('silver')

은색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 은색 (銀色), joining 은 (銀, 'silver metal') and 색 (色, 'color, hue').

은행길.etymology: Compound street name formed from Sino-Korean 은행 (either 銀杏 'ginkgo tree' or 銀行 'bank') + native Korean 길 ('road, street, way') — 'Ginkgo Street' or 'Bank Street'.

을.etymology: Native Korean accusative (direct object) case particle attached to consonant-final nouns (allomorph of 를 after vowels), descending from Middle Korean 을 / 알.

음.etymology: Represents both Sino-Korean 음 (音, 'sound, tone, musical note, pronunciation') and the natural Korean nasal vocalization 음 ('hmm, well', uttered while pondering or agreeing).

history.meaning: sound, musical pitch, speech sound; also contemplative interjection ('hmm')

음계.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 음계 (音階), joining 음 (音, 'sound, musical note') and 계 (階, 'steps, stairs, gradations') — literally 'staircase of notes'.

음성.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음성 (音聲), uniting 음 (音, 'sound') and 성 (聲, 'voice').
음성.notes: Used in technical or formal contexts like 음성 메시지 ('voice message'), whereas native 목소리 is everyday spoken 'voice'.

음악.notes: The everyday word for music of any kind.

음악회.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음악회 (音樂會), joining 음악 (音樂, 'music', from 音 'sound' + 樂 'music') and 회 (會, 'gathering, assembly, recital').

음표.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음표 (音標), combining 음 (音, 'sound, musical tone') and 표 (標, 'mark, symbol').
음표.notes: Shares 음 (音) with 음악 ('music') and 표 (標) with 화살표 ('arrow mark').

음향.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 음향 (音響), joining 음 (音, 'sound, tone') and 향 (響, 'echo, resonance, reverberation').

의자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 의자 (椅子), joining 의 (椅, 'catalpa tree; wooden chair with a backrest') and diminutive/nominal suffix 자 (子).

이.etymology: Native Korean proximal demonstrative determiner ('this', Middle Korean 이), post-consonantal nominative case particle (-이), and native noun 이 ('tooth', Middle Korean 니); also Sino-Korean numeral 이 (二, 'two').

이거.etymology: Colloquial spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing, this one'), formed from proximal demonstrative 이 ('this') + bound noun 거 (< 것 'thing').

이것.etymology: Native Korean compound demonstrative pronoun descending from Middle Korean 이것, formed from proximal determiner 이 ('this') + bound noun 것 ('thing, object').

이겨내다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 이기다 ('to win, overcome', conjunctive 이겨) + completive auxiliary verb 내다 ('to carry through to the end, manage to').

history.meaning: to overcome, endure and triumph over a hardship

이기다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 이기다 ('to win, defeat an opponent, master, knead dough thoroughly').

이다.etymology: Native Korean predicative copula ('to be [something]') descending from Middle Korean 이라 / 이다, attaching directly to nouns; also a homonymous native verb 이다 ('to carry on the head; to roof a house').

history.meaning: predicative copula ('to be'); also 'to carry on the head'

이런.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner contracted from 이러하- (이렇다, 'to be like this, be such') + adnominal suffix -ㄴ; also used as a mild exclamation of surprise or regret ('oh dear, my goodness').

이렇게.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 이러하게, adverbial form (-게) of 이러하다 / 이렇다 ('to be like this').

history.meaning: like this, in this way, so

이렇다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb contracted from 이러하다 (Middle Korean 이러하다, 'to be like this, be so', built on proximal deictic root 이-).

history.meaning: to be like this, be so

이르다.etymology: Convergence of three native Korean verbs from distinct Middle Korean stems: (1) adjective 이르다 ('to be early', Middle Korean 이르다); (2) verb 이르다 ('to reach, arrive at', Middle Korean 니르다, ל-irregular); and (3) verb 이르다 ('to say, tell, inform on', Middle Korean 니르다).

history.meaning: to be early; to reach a place; to tell or report

이름.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 일홈 ('name, appellation'), nominalization in -옴/-움 of 니르다 / 일컫다 ('to call, name, say').

history.meaning: that by which something is called, name

이름표.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 이름 ('name') + Sino-Korean 표 (票/標, 'tag, label, ticket').

이리.etymology: Native Korean directional/manner adverb descending from Middle Korean 이리 ('this way, toward here; in this manner'), formed from proximal demonstrative root 이- + directional suffix -리.

history.meaning: this way, over here; thus, so

이마.etymology: Native Korean anatomical noun descending from Middle Korean 니마ㅎ ('forehead, brow').

이백팔십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이백팔십 (二百八十), joining 이백 (二百, 'two hundred') and 팔십 (八十, 'eighty').

이번.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean proximal determiner 이 ('this') + Sino-Korean counter 번 (番, 'turn, time, occasion').

history.meaning: this time, this occasion, the current...

이불장.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from native Korean 이불 ('bedding quilt, comforter', Middle Korean 니블, from 닙다/입다 'to cover, wear') + Sino-Korean 장 (欌, 'wardrobe, cabinet, chest').

history.meaning: bedding closet or wardrobe for storing quilts and blankets

이삿짐센터.etymology: Three-part hybrid compound combining Sino-Korean 이사 (移徙, 'moving house, relocation', from 移 'to move' + 徙 'to shift residence') + compound interfix -ㅅ- + native Korean 짐 ('luggage, household load') + English loanword 센터 (center).

이상하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb formed from Sino-Korean 이상 (異常, 'unusualness, abnormality', from 異 'different, strange' + 常 'ordinary, constant') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.form: 異常 (이상, 'different from the norm') + -하다 -> 이상하다
history.meaning: to be strange, odd, unusual, weird

이슬비.etymology: Native Korean compound of 이슬 ('morning dew') and 비 ('rain').
이슬비.notes: Evokes a mist-like drizzle gentler than 소나기 ('passing shower') or 폭우 ('downpour').

이십.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이십 (二十), joining 이 (二, 'two') and 십 (十, 'ten').

이십구.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이십구 (二十九), joining 이십 (二十, 'twenty') and 구 (九, 'nine').

이야기.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Early Modern Korean 니야기 / 이야기 ('story, tale, conversation', likely derived from 니르다 'to tell, speak').

이야기하다.etymology: Native Korean verb formed from 이야기 ('story, talk, conversation') + light verb -하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to talk, converse, tell a story

이웃.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 이우즛 / 이웃 ('neighbor, neighboring house', related to 잇다 'to join, connect consecutively').

이유.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이유 (理由), joining 리/이 (理, 'principle, reason, logic') and 유 (由, 'cause, origin, from').

이음새.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 이음 ('joining, connection', verbal noun in -음 of 잇다 'to join, link together') + suffix -새 ('manner, appearance, seam').

history.meaning: joint, seam, point where two pieces are joined

이전.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이전 (以前, 'before this, previous times', from 以 'by, from' + 前 'before, prior'; also 移轉 'moving to a new location, transfer of rights').

history.meaning: prior time, before; relocation or transfer

이제.etymology: Native Korean temporal noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 이제 ('now, this moment', formed from proximal demonstrative 이 'this' + 적/제 'time, occasion').

이제야.etymology: Native Korean emphatic temporal adverb formed from 이제 ('now') + emphatic particle -야 ('only when, at last').

이중주.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 이중주 (二重奏), joining 이 (二, 'two'), 중 (重, 'fold, layer'), and 주 (奏, 'musical performance') — literally 'two-part instrumental performance'.

이천.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral compound 이천 (二千), joining 이 (二, 'two') and 천 (千, 'thousand').

이층.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이층 (二層), joining 이 (二, 'two') and 층 (層, 'story, level, floor').

이틀.etymology: Native Korean day-count noun descending from Middle Korean 이틀 ('two days; the second day of the month', built on an archaic native root 이트- 'two' + 날 'day').

history.meaning: two days; second day of a month

이해하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 이해 (理解, 'understanding, comprehension', from 理 'principle, reason' + 解 'to untie, loosen, solve') + native verb suffix -하다.

이후.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 이후 (以後), joining 이 (以, 'from, by') and 후 (後, 'after, behind, later').

history.meaning: after this, from then on, afterward, since

익다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 익다 ('to ripen, become thoroughly cooked, ferment, become familiar or skilled through practice').

history.meaning: to ripen, cook through, become practiced
to ripen, be cooked, grow familiar

익숙하다.etymology: Hybrid descriptive verb combining the native Korean verb stem 익- (익다, 'to grow familiar or practiced') + Sino-Korean 숙 (熟, 'ripe, cooked, skilled, familiar') + native adjective suffix -하다 — a tautological native + Sino-Korean synonym compound.

history.meaning: to be accustomed to, familiar with, skilled at

인사하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from Sino-Korean 인사 (人事, originally 'human affairs, social courtesy and etiquette', from 人 'person' + 事 'affair, service') + native verb suffix -하다.

history.meaning: to greet, bow in greeting, say hello or goodbye

인생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 인생 (人生), joining 인 (人, 'human being, person') and 생 (生, 'life, birth, living').

일.etymology: Convergence of two high-frequency words: (1) native Korean noun 일 ('work, task, matter, event', descending from Middle Korean 일); and (2) Sino-Korean numeral 일 (一, 'one') or calendar counter 일 (日, 'day').

일곱.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean 닐굽 ('seven').

일기예보.etymology: Four-character Sino-Korean compound 일기예보 (日氣豫報), joining 일기 (日氣, 'daily weather') with 예보 (豫報, 'advance report, forecast').
일기예보.notes: Standard broadcast and everyday term for a weather forecast.

일부러.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Early Modern Korean 일부러 ('on purpose, intentionally, going out of one's way').

일어나다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 니러나다, formed from 일다 ('to rise, spring up', Middle Korean 닐다) + 나다 ('to come out, occur, happen').

history.meaning: to rise up, wake up, occur
to get up (from sleep or sitting), stand up, happen/break out

일어서다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 니러서다, formed from 일다 ('to rise', Middle Korean 닐다) + 서다 ('to stand').

history.meaning: to stand up, rise to one's feet

일요일.etymology: Sino-Korean calendar compound 일요일 (日曜日), joining 일 (日, 'Sun'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day') — literally 'Day of the Sun' (Sunday).

일주일.etymology: Sino-Korean temporal compound 일주일 (一週日), joining 일 (一, 'one'), 주 (週, 'cycle, week'), and 일 (日, 'day').

일찍.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 일즉 ('early, betimes; formerly', derived from the stem of 이르다 'to be early').

일층.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 일층 (一層), joining 일 (一, 'one, first') and 층 (層, 'story, floor, layer').

일하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb descending from Middle Korean 일하다, formed from 일 ('work, labor') + 하다 ('to do').

일호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 일호실 (一號室), joining 일 (一, 'one, No. 1'), 호 (號, 'number, designation'), and 실 (室, 'room').

읽다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 닑다 ('to read aloud, recite, peruse written characters').

읽히다.etymology: Native Korean passive and causative verb descending from Middle Korean 닑히다, formed from 읽다 ('to read') + suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be read (easily or widely); to have someone read

잃어버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 잃다 ('to lose', Middle Korean 잃다) + completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to end up doing completely, regrettably').

history.meaning: to lose completely, misplace for good

임대.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 임대 (賃貸), joining 임 (賃, 'to hire, rent for payment') and 대 (貸, 'to lend, lease out').

history.meaning: leasing out, rental (of real estate or equipment)

입.etymology: Native Korean anatomical noun descending from Middle Korean 입 ('mouth, lips, opening').

입구.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 입구 (入口), joining 입 (入, 'to enter, go in') and 구 (口, 'mouth, opening, gate') — literally 'entering mouth/opening'.

입다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 닙다 ('to put on or wear clothing on the body; to receive a favor or suffer damage').

history.meaning: to wear clothing; to receive or suffer
to wear, put on (clothes); to suffer (harm) or receive (grace)

있다.etymology: Native Korean existential and possessive verb/adjective descending from Middle Korean 이시다 ('to exist, be in a place, have, stay').

history.meaning: to be (in a place), exist, have

잉크.etymology: Modern loanword borrowed from English ink (ultimately via Old French enque from Late Latin encaustum < Ancient Greek enkauston 'purple ink burned in').

잊다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 잊다 ('to forget, let slip from memory').

잊어버리다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 잊다 ('to forget') + completive auxiliary verb 버리다 ('to end up doing completely').

잎사귀.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Early Modern Korean 닙사귀 / 입사귀, derived from 잎 ('leaf', Middle Korean 닢) + suffix -사귀 ('foliage, individual leaf blade', cf. 귀 'ear, corner').

자.etymology: Native Koreanhortative/prompting interjection 자 ('come on!, well now!, here we go!'); also a native Korean noun 자 ('measuring ruler, Korean foot measure', Middle Korean 자ㅎ).

history.meaning: well!, come now!, here! (interj.); ruler, foot measure (noun)

자국.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 자국 / 자최 ('footprint, track, mark or stain left behind where something has pressed or passed').

history.meaning: footprint, track, trace, mark, scar, stain

자기.etymology: Sino-Korean reflexive pronoun 자기 (自己), joining 자 (自, 'self, oneself') and 기 (己, 'self, one's own person'); also used in modern colloquial Korean as an affectionate second-person pronoun between romantic partners ('honey, darling').

자꾸.etymology: Native Korean adverb (attested in Early Modern Korean 자고 / 자꾸) meaning 'repeatedly, over and over, persistently'.

자다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 자다 ('to sleep, go to bed').

history.meaning: to sleep, lodge for the night; (of a clock) to stop

자라나다.etymology: Native Korean compound intransitive verb formed from 자라다 ('to grow, mature', Middle Korean 자라다) + 나다 ('to come forth, sprout, develop').

history.meaning: to grow up, spring up and mature

자라다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 자라다 ('to grow in size or age, mature; to be sufficient').

history.meaning: to grow up, grow (of plants, animals, children)

자르다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 짤아다 / 자르다 ('to cut off, sever, chop into pieces').

자리.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 자리 ('woven mat for sitting or sleeping; seat, place, spot, position, trace').

history.meaning: seat, place, spot, job opening, occasion

자물쇠.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 자믈쇠, formed from the verb stem 잠그- / 자믈- ('to lock, fasten shut', Middle Korean 자믈다) + 쇠 ('iron, metal device').

자세히.etymology: Hybrid adverb formed from Sino-Korean 자세 (仔細 / 詳細, 'minute, detailed, attentive', from 仔 'careful, minute' + 細 'fine, small, detailed') + native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

작가.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작가 (作家), joining 작 (作, 'to make, compose, write, create') and specialist suffix 가 (家, 'master, specialist, school').

작가님.etymology: Polite title formed from Sino-Korean 작가 (作家, 'writer, author, artist') + native Korean honorific suffix -님.

작곡가.etymology: Three-part Sino-Korean compound 작곡가 (作曲家): 작 (作, 'make, create') + 곡 (曲, 'tune, piece of music') + specialist suffix -가 (家).
작곡가.notes: Parallels 건축가 (建築家, 'architect') in using -가 (家) for an accomplished practitioner.

작곡가님.etymology: Polite title formed from Sino-Korean 작곡가 (作曲家, 'musical composer', from 作 'make, compose' + 曲 'melody, tune' + 家 'specialist') + native Korean honorific suffix -님.

history.meaning: esteemed musical composer (polite address or reference)

작다.etymology: Native Korean descriptive verb descending from Middle Korean 쟉다 ('to be small in size, short in height, minor', bright-vowel counterpart of 적다 'to be few in number/quantity').

history.meaning: to be small, little, low in volume

작업.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작업 (作業), joining 작 (作, 'to make, work, operate') and 업 (業, 'work, occupation, task').

history.meaning: work, operation, hands-on job or task

작업실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 작업실 (作業室), joining 작업 (作業, 'work, artistic or manual craft') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

잔.etymology: Sino-Korean 잔 (盞, 'small cup, winecup, glass'), borrowed from Middle Chinese 盞 ('shallow cup, goblet') and used both as an independent noun ('cup, glass') and as a counter for drinks.

잘.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean 잘 ('well, skillfully, properly, often').

잘되다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the adverb 잘 ('well, successfully') and the verb 되다 ('to become, turn out, go').

history.meaning: to go well, turn out successfully, prosper

잘못.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from the adverbs 잘 ('well, properly') and 못 ('cannot, poorly, amiss'), lexicalized both as a noun ('mistake, fault, error') and as an adverb ('wrongly, mistakenly').

잘하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the adverb 잘 ('well, skillfully') and the verb 하다 ('to do, perform').

history.meaning: to do well, be good at, treat well

잠그다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ㅭᆞᆷ그다 / 잠그다 ('to immerse in liquid, steep; to shut and lock').

history.meaning: to lock, fasten, turn off (a valve); to soak

잠기다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from 잠그다 ('to lock; to immerse') + the passive suffix -이-, attested in Middle Korean as ㅭᆞᆷ기다 / 잠기다.

history.meaning: to be submerged; to be locked
to be locked, fastened; to sink, be immersed

잠깐.etymology: Phonologically tensified form of Sino-Korean 잠간 (暫間), compounding 잠 (暫, 'briefly, temporarily') and 간 (間, 'interval, space of time').

history.meaning: for a moment, briefly; just a second

잠시.etymology: Sino-Korean 잠시 (暫時), compounding 잠 (暫, 'briefly, for a short time') and 시 (時, 'time, period').

history.meaning: a short while, a moment; briefly

잡다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 잡다 ('to grasp, hold, catch, seize').

history.meaning: to catch, hold, grip, set (a date or plan)

장.etymology: Sino-Korean monosyllable representing several common homographs: 장 (場, 'place, ground, market'), 장 (欌, 'cabinet, wardrobe'), 장 (張, classifier for flat sheets such as paper or leaves), and 장 (章, 'chapter, section').

history.form: 場 / 欌 / 張 / 章 (장)
history.meaning: market, place / cabinet / sheet counter / chapter

장난감.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 장난 ('play, pastime, prank', attested in early Modern Korean as 작난) + the suffixoid/noun 감 ('material, item suitable for a purpose').

장난치다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 장난 ('play, prank, mischief') + 치다 ('to strike, make, engage in').

history.meaning: to play a prank, fool around, joke

장담하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 장담 (壯談, 'bold talk, confident assurance', compounding 壯 'vigorous, bold' and 談 'talk, speech') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to assure confidently, guarantee, vouch for

장바구니.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 장 (場, 'market, marketplace, grocery shopping') + native Korean 바구니 ('woven basket').

history.meaning: market basket, shopping bag or cart

장부.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 장부 (帳簿), combining 장 (帳, 'account register') and 부 (簿, 'record book, ledger').
장부.notes: Used for traditional paper account books and guesthouse check-in ledgers.

장인.etymology: Sino-Korean 장인 (匠人), from 장 (匠, 'artisan, master woodworker') + 인 (人, 'person').
장인.notes: Honors a craftsperson who has dedicated decades to perfecting a manual craft.

재개장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 재개장 (再開場), joining prefix 재- (再, 'again, re-') with 개장 (開場, 'opening a venue').
재개장.notes: Used for guesthouses, theatres, markets, and halls opening their doors anew.

재능.etymology: Sino-Korean 재능 (才能), compounding 재 (才, 'natural gift, talent') and 능 (能, 'ability, capability, skill').

재다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 재다 ('to measure length, size, or quantity; to gauge').

재벌칠.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean prefix 재- (再, 'second time, again') + native Korean 벌 ('round, layer, set') + Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, paint, coating'), denoting a second coat of paint or plaster.

history.meaning: second coat of paint, varnish, or plaster

재생.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 재생 (再生), combining 재 (再, 'again, a second time') and 생 (生, 'come alive, produce').
재생.notes: Means both ecological/material regeneration ('recycling, renewal') and audio/video playback ('bringing recorded sound back to life').

재작년.etymology: Sino-Korean 재작년 (再昨年), formed from prefix 재- (再, 'again, one step further back') + 작년 (昨年, 'last year', from 昨 'yesterday, past' + 年 'year').

잼.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English jam ('sweet fruit preserve boiled with sugar').

쟁반.etymology: Sino-Korean 쟁반 (錚盤), compounding 쟁 (錚, 'clang of metal, flat metal gong or plate') and 반 (盤, 'tray, platter, shallow basin').

저.etymology: In humble first-person usage ('I, me'), native Korean pronoun descending from Middle Korean 뎌 / 저 ('oneself; humble I'); as a distal demonstrative ('that over there'), from Middle Korean 뎌 ('that').

history.meaning: oneself, humble I / that over there

저거.etymology: Colloquial contracted form of 저것 ('that thing over there'), composed of distal demonstrative 저 ('that') + 거 (reduced form of dependent noun 것 'thing').

저것.etymology: Native Korean compound pronoun formed from distal demonstrative 저 ('that over there', Middle Korean 뎌) + the bound noun 것 ('thing, object').

history.meaning: that thing, that one (away from both speaker and listener)

저기.etymology: Native Korean distal locative pronoun descending from Middle Korean 뎌긔 ('that place over there', from distal 뎌 + locative nominal element -긔).

history.meaning: over there, that place; excuse me (attention-getter)

저녁.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 져녁 ('evening, dusk; evening meal').

저런.etymology: Native Korean determiner contracted from 저러한 ('such as that over there', from distal demonstrative stem 저러- + -하- + adnominal -ㄴ); also used as an exclamation of surprise or sympathy ('oh dear, my goodness').

history.meaning: that kind of, such; oh my!

저렇다.etymology: Native Korean demonstrative adjective contracted from 저러하다 ('to be like that over there'), descending from Middle Korean 뎌러하다 (built on distal root 뎌- 'that').

history.meaning: to be like that (over there), be that way

저분.etymology: Native Korean honorific pronoun formed from distal demonstrative 저 ('that over there') + the honorific bound noun 분 ('esteemed person').

저희.etymology: Native Korean humble first-person plural pronoun ('we, us, our') descending from Middle Korean 저희, formed from 저 ('oneself; humble I') + the animate plural suffix -희.

적.etymology: As a native Korean bound noun ('the time when, occasion, past experience'), descending from Middle Korean 젹 ('time, occasion'); as an independent Sino-Korean noun ('enemy, foe, rival'), borrowed from 적 (敵).

적다.etymology: As a verb ('to write down, note, record'), native Korean descending from Middle Korean 젹다 ('to write down'); homophonous with the native Korean adjective 적다 ('to be few, small in quantity', Middle Korean 쟉다 / 젹다).

history.meaning: to write down, record; to be few, little
to write down, jot down; to be few, little

적시다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 젹시다 ('to make wet, moisten, soak'), historically related to 젖다 ('to get wet').

적히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 적다 ('to write down, record') + the passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be written down, be recorded, be listed

전.etymology: Primarily Sino-Korean 전 (前, 'front, before, former, ago'); also represents Sino-Korean 전 (全, 'whole, complete') and 전 (煎, 'pan-fried battered food, savoury pancake').

history.meaning: before, ago, former; whole; Korean savoury pancake

전구.etymology: Sino-Korean 전구 (電球), compounding 전 (電, 'electricity, lightning') and 구 (球, 'ball, sphere, globe').

전등.etymology: Sino-Korean 전등 (電燈), compounding 전 (電, 'electricity') and 등 (燈, 'lamp, lantern, light').

전등갓.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 전등 (電燈, 'electric lamp') + native Korean 갓 ('conical hat, canopy, shade', Middle Korean 갈 / 갓).

전망.etymology: Sino-Korean 전망 (展望), compounding 전 (展, 'unfold, open up, spread out') and 망 (望, 'look into the distance, view, hope').

전부.etymology: Sino-Korean 전부 (全部), compounding 전 (全, 'whole, entire, complete') and 부 (部, 'part, section, division').

전선.etymology: Sino-Korean 전선 (電線), compounding 전 (電, 'electricity') and 선 (線, 'line, thread, wire'); also homophonous with 전선 (戰線, 'battlefront, front line').

전역.etymology: Sino-Korean 전역 (全域, 'the entire area, whole region'), compounding 전 (全, 'whole, entire') and 역 (域, 'region, territory, boundary'); also homophonous with 전역 (轉役, 'transfer to the reserves, discharge from military service').

history.meaning: the whole area, throughout; completion of military service

전체.etymology: Sino-Korean 전체 (全體), compounding 전 (全, 'whole, complete, entire') and 체 (體, 'body, substance, system').

전하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 전 (傳, 'to transmit, hand down, pass on, deliver') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to convey, deliver, tell, pass on

전혀.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 전 (全, 'wholly, completely') + the native Korean adverbial suffix -혀, attested in Middle Korean as 젼혀 ('entirely, completely', now used predominantly with negative predicates to mean 'not at all').

전화.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 전화 (電話), literally 'electric speech', coined in East Asia for the telephone.
전화.notes: Combines into 전화기 ('telephone set') and 전화번호 ('phone number').

전화기.etymology: Sino-Korean 전화기 (電話機), formed from 전화 (電話, 'telephone', from 電 'electricity' + 話 'speech, conversation') + 기 (機, 'machine, device, apparatus').

전화번호.etymology: Sino-Korean 전화번호 (電話番號), compounding 전화 (電話, 'telephone') and 번호 (番號, 'number, numerical code', from 番 'turn, order' + 號 'mark, number').

전화하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 전화 (電話, 'telephone, phone call') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to make a phone call, telephone

전환.etymology: Sino-Korean 전환 (轉換), compounding 전 (轉, 'turn, revolve, shift') and 환 (換, 'exchange, replace, switch').

전환하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 전환 (轉換, 'conversion, switch, shift') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

절대.etymology: Sino-Korean 절대 (絕對), compounding 절 (絕, 'cut off, sever, surpass') and 대 (對, 'oppose, pair, compare'), originally a Buddhist philosophical term meaning 'beyond all comparison or relative opposition, absolute'.

history.meaning: absoluteness; absolutely, by no means (with negation)

절반.etymology: Sino-Korean 절반 (折半), compounding 절 (折, 'break, fold, divide') and 반 (半, 'half').

절연.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 절연 (絶緣), from 절 (絶, 'sever, cut off') and 연 (緣, 'tie, connection, edge').
절연.notes: Means severing personal ties in literary prose, and blocking electrical current ('insulation') in engineering.

젊다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 졈다 ('to be young, youthful').

점.etymology: Sino-Korean 점 (點, 'dot, spot, point, mark, aspect, score; counter for artworks or items'); also represents 점 (店, 'shop, store') and 점 (占, 'divination, fortune-telling').

history.meaning: point, dot, mole, score, aspect; store; fortune-telling

점검.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 점검 (點檢), from 점 (點, 'dot, itemize, check off') and 검 (檢, 'inspect, verify').
점검.notes: Originally meant checking off items one dot at a time on an inventory roll.

점검하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 점검 (點檢, 'checking item by item, inspection', compounding 點 'dot, check off' and 檢 'examine, inspect') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do').

점수.etymology: Sino-Korean 점수 (點數), compounding 점 (點, 'point, mark') and 수 (數, 'number, count').

점심.etymology: Sino-Korean 점심 (點心), compounding 점 (點, 'dot, touch lightly') and 심 (心, 'heart, mind'), originally a Chinese and Zen monastic term meaning 'to stay the stomach with a light midday refreshment' (cognate with Cantonese dim sum).

history.meaning: light refreshment to touch the heart/stomach

접다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 졉다 ('to fold, double over').

history.meaning: to fold, collapse; to set aside or give up

접시.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 뎌프시 / 졉시 ('shallow plate, saucer, dish').

접이식.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 접이 ('folding', derived from 접다 'to fold' + nominalizer -이) + Sino-Korean 식 (式, 'style, type, system').

접질리다.etymology: Native Korean verb meaning 'to sprain, twist (a joint under pressure)', derived from the root of 접다 ('to fold, bend back') with intensive and passive suffixation.

history.meaning: to sprain, wrench, twist (an ankle, wrist, etc.)

접히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 접다 ('to fold') + the passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be folded, fold up, crease

젓다.etymology: Native Korean s-irregular verb (젓-, 저어) descending from Middle Korean 졋다 ('to stir, churn; to row with an oar; to wave or shake').

history.meaning: to stir; to row; to wave
to stir; to row a boat; to shake one's head or wave one's hand

정.etymology: Primarily Sino-Korean 정 (情, 'warmth, affection, emotional bond, attachment, sympathy'); also represents native/Sino-Korean 정 (錠, 'chisel, burin; tablet').

정각.etymology: Sino-Korean 정각 (正刻), compounding 정 (正, 'exact, right, straight') and 각 (刻, 'carved notch on a clepsydra, time mark, moment').

history.meaning: the exact hour, o'clock sharp, on the dot

정도.etymology: Sino-Korean 정도 (程度), compounding 정 (程, 'measure, standard, stage, journey') and 도 (度, 'degree, measure, limit').

정말.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 정 (正, 'right, true, genuine') + native Korean 말 ('word, speech, talk'), literally 'true words, truth', used both as a noun and as an adverb ('really, truly').

정성껏.etymology: Hybrid adverb formed from Sino-Korean 정성 (精誠, 'true heart, utmost sincerity and devotion', from 精 'pure, refined' + 誠 'sincerity') + the native Korean suffix -껏 ('to the utmost of').

history.meaning: with all one's heart, wholeheartedly, with utmost care

정숙도.etymology: Sino-Korean 정숙도 (靜肅度), formed from 정숙 (靜肅, 'quietness, silence, stillness', from 靜 'quiet, still' + 肅 'solemn, hushed') + the suffix 도 (度, 'degree, level').

history.meaning: degree of quietness, noise-insulation or hush level

정식.etymology: Represents two common Sino-Korean compounds: 정식 (正式, 'formal, official, proper form', from 正 'right, proper' + 式 'form, style, ceremony') and 정식 (定食, 'fixed set meal, table d'hôte', from 定 'fixed, settled' + 食 'meal, food').

history.meaning: proper official form / fixed set meal
formality, official way; set meal, full-course meal

정오.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 정오 (正午), from 정 (正, 'exact, upright') and 오 (午, 'the Horse hour', 11 a.m.–1 p.m., whose midpoint is twelve noon).
정오.notes: Explains 오전 (午前, 'before noon / a.m.') and 오후 (午後, 'after noon / p.m.') as well.

정원.etymology: Sino-Korean 정원 (庭園, 'garden, landscaped yard'), compounding 정 (庭, 'courtyard, yard') and 원 (園, 'garden, orchard, park'); also homophonous with 정원 (定員, 'fixed capacity or quota of people').

history.meaning: courtyard and garden / fixed number of personnel

정원용.etymology: Sino-Korean 정원용 (庭園用), formed from 정원 (庭園, 'garden') + the suffix 용 (用, 'use, intended for').

정직원.etymology: Sino-Korean 정직원 (正職員), formed from prefix 정- (正, 'regular, official, full-time') + 직원 (職員, 'staff member, employee', from 職 'post, duty' + 員 'member, personnel').

history.meaning: regular full-time employee, permanent staff member

정직하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정직 (正直, 'honesty, uprightness, candor', compounding 正 'right, straight' and 直 'straight, direct, honest') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

정하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정 (定, 'to fix, settle, decide, establish') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

정해지다.etymology: Passive/inchoative verb formed from 정하다 ('to decide, set', from Sino-Korean 定 + 하다) + the auxiliary passive construction -아/어지다 ('to become, come to be').

history.meaning: to be decided, be set, be determined

정확하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정확 (正確, 'accuracy, precision, exactness', compounding 正 'right, correct' and 確 'firm, certain, accurate') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

정확히.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 정확 (正確, 'accurate, exact') + the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

젖다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 젗다 ('to get wet, become soaked or damp').

history.meaning: to get wet, be soaked; to be steeped in (an emotion)

제.etymology: Primarily the contracted possessive and pre-가 nominative form of humble first-person 저 ('I, my') or reflexive 저 ('one's own', Middle Korean 졔 < 저 + 의/이); also represents Sino-Korean ordinal prefix 제- (第-, 'number, -th').

history.meaning: my (humble) / one's own; I (before subject marker)
my (humble), one's own; I (before 가); ordinal prefix (第)

제대로.etymology: Native Korean adverb lexicalized from reflexive 제 ('its own proper [state or form]') + the particle/bound noun 대로 ('in accordance with, just as').

history.meaning: as it should be, properly,in good order

제목.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 제목 (題目), combining 제 (題, 'forehead, heading, inscription') and 목 (目, 'eye, item, heading').
제목.notes: Standard word for the title of a piece of sheet music, book, or article.

제발.etymology: Attested since early Modern Korean as 데발 / 제발 ('please, I beg of you'); generally traced to Sino-Korean 제발 (濟拔, a Buddhist term meaning 'to save and pull out from suffering', from 濟 'save, ferry across' + 拔 'pull out, rescue').

제빵.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean prefix 제- (製, 'making, manufacturing') + 빵 ('bread', borrowed via Japanese pan from Portuguese pão < Latin pānis).

제빵사.etymology: A compound of Sino-Korean 제 (製) 'make', 빵 'bread' and Sino-Korean 사 (師) 'master, specialist'.

제일.etymology: Sino-Korean 제일 (第一), compounding the ordinal prefix 제- (第, 'rank, order') and 일 (一, 'one, first'), used both as a noun ('number one, the first') and as a superlative adverb ('most, best').

제자리.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from the reflexive determiner 제 ('its own, one's own') + 자리 ('place, spot, seat, position').

history.meaning: its own place, original position, right spot

조.etymology: Sino-Korean monosyllable representing several common homographs: 조 (組, 'group, team, squad, set'), 조 (條, 'article, clause, item'), and 조 (兆, 'one trillion; omen'); also native Korean 조 ('foxtail millet', Middle Korean 조).

history.meaning: group, team / article, clause / trillion, omen
group, team; legal article; trillion; millet

조각.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 조각 ('broken piece, fragment, slice, shard'); homophonous with Sino-Korean 조각 (彫刻, 'carving, sculpture').

조금.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 조ᄀᆞᆷ ('a little, a small amount, slightly').

조례.etymology: Represents two Sino-Korean compounds: 조례 (條例, 'municipal ordinance, bylaw, regulation', from 條 'article, clause' + 例 'rule, regulation') and 조례 (朝禮, 'morning assembly or briefing', from 朝 'morning' + 禮 'ceremony, greeting').

조리대.etymology: Sino-Korean 조리대 (調理臺), formed from 조리 (調理, 'cooking, culinary preparation', from 調 'season, harmonize' + 理 'arrange, prepare') + 대 (臺, 'platform, stand, counter').

조명.etymology: Sino-Korean 조명 (照明), compounding 조 (照, 'shine, illuminate') and 명 (明, 'bright, light').

조성.etymology: Sino-Korean musical compound 조성 (調性), from 조 (調, 'melody, tune, key') and 성 (性, 'nature, quality').
조성.notes: Distinguishes musical tonality/key from unrelated homographs of 조.

조심하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 조심 (操心, 'caution, heedfulness', literally 'holding and governing one's mind', from 操 'hold, control' + 心 'mind, heart') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: to govern one's mind, exercise caution
to be careful, watch out, take care

조용하다.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 종용 (從容, 'calm, unhurried, quiet, composed'), attested in Middle Korean as 죵용ᄒᆞ다 and evolving by dissimilation of the first nasal coda to 조용하다.

조용히.etymology: Formed from the root of 조용하다 ('to be quiet, calm' < Sino-Korean 從容) + the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

조율.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 조율 (調律), combining 조 (調, 'adjust, harmonize') and 율 (律, 'musical pitch, standard').
조율.notes: Used both literally for tuning stringed instruments and figuratively for coordinating plans.

조율하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 조율 (調律, 'tuning musical pitches; coordinating differing views', compounding 調 'harmonize, adjust' and 律 'musical pitch, standard') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: to tune (an instrument); to coordinate, mediate, fine-tune

조이다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 조이다 / 조히다 ('to tighten, bind fast, make taut; to feel anxious').

history.meaning: to tighten, fasten firmly, screw down

조합.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 조합 (組合), from 조 (組, 'braid, group, pair') and 합 (合, 'join, unite').
조합.notes: Common in food talk for a winning flavour pairing (꿀조합, 좋은 조합).

존경하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 존경 (尊敬, 'respect, reverence, esteem', compounding 尊 'honor, revere' and 敬 'respect, venerate') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: to respect, look up to, esteem

존댓말.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 존대 (尊待, 'respectful treatment or address', from 尊 'honor' + 待 'treat') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + native Korean 말 ('speech, words, language').

좀.etymology: Native Korean adverb contracted from 조금 ('a little, a bit'), attested since early Modern Korean and frequently used as a politeness softener ('please, just a bit').

좁다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 좁다 ('to be narrow, cramped, small in width or area').

종.etymology: Sino-Korean 종 (鐘, 'bell, chime'); also represents Sino-Korean 종 (種, 'kind, species, type') and native Korean 종 ('servant, slave', Middle Korean 죵).

종소리.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 종 (鐘, 'bell') + native Korean 소리 ('sound, voice, ringing').

history.meaning: sound of a bell, bell tolling or chiming

종이.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 죠ᄒᆡ ('paper'), evolving through 죠희 > 조히 > 종이.

좋다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 둗다 ('to be good, fine, desirable'), which underwent palatalization of initial ㄷ before ㅛ in early Modern Korean (둗다 > 죻다 > 좋다).

좋아하다.etymology: Native Korean psychological verb formed from the adjective 좋다 ('to be good, pleasing') + the auxiliary verb construction -아 하다 ('to feel or consider [something] good, to like').

history.meaning: to like, rejoice in, be fond of
to like, be fond of, enjoy

죄송하다.etymology: Derived from Sino-Korean 죄송 (罪悚, literally 'guilty and fearful') combined with 하다.
죄송하다.notes: Standard polite expression for 'I am sorry' toward guests, strangers, and elders; casual speech prefers native 미안하다.

주.etymology: Primarily Sino-Korean 주 (週, 'week, seven-day cycle'); also represents Sino-Korean 주 (州, 'state, province'), 주 (株, 'share of stock'), and 주 (主, 'master, main').

history.form: 週 / 州 / 株 / 主 (주)
history.meaning: week / province, state / stock share / master, main

주다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 주다 ('to give, hand over, bestow'), also widely used as a benefactive auxiliary verb (-아/어 주다).

history.meaning: to give; to do something for someone (auxiliary)

주로.etymology: Hybrid adverb lexicalized from Sino-Korean 주 (主, 'main, chief, principal part') + the native Korean instrumental particle -로 ('by way of, as').

history.meaning: mainly, mostly, chiefly, for the most part

주말.etymology: Sino-Korean 주말 (週末), compounding 주 (週, 'week') and 말 (末, 'end, close').

주머니.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 주머귀 ('small drawstring pouch, bag, purse'), evolving to modern 주머니.

주무시다.etymology: Native Korean honorific verb ('to sleep') descending from Middle Korean 주무시다, historically formed with the honorific suffix -시-.

history.meaning: to sleep, go to bed (honorific of 자다)

주문하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 주문 (注文, 'placing an order for goods or food, request', from 注 'fix upon, note down' + 文 'writing, text') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: to order (food, goods), place an order

주민.etymology: Sino-Korean 주민 (住民), compounding 주 (住, 'dwell, reside, live') and 민 (民, 'people, inhabitants').

주방.etymology: Sino-Korean 주방 (廚房), compounding 주 (廚, 'kitchen, cookhouse') and 방 (房, 'room, chamber').

주소.etymology: Sino-Korean 주소 (住所), compounding 주 (住, 'dwell, reside') and 소 (所, 'place, location').

주스.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English juice ('liquid pressed from fruit or vegetables').

주인.etymology: Sino-Korean 주인 (主人), compounding 주 (主, 'master, owner, host') and 인 (人, 'person').

history.meaning: master of the house, host, owner

주인공.etymology: Sino-Korean 주인공 (主人公), formed from 주인 (主人, 'master, host') + 공 (公, honorific title 'lord, respected figure'), originally a Zen Buddhist term for one's true inner master and in modern Korean 'main character, protagonist'.

주전자.etymology: Sino-Korean 주전자 (酒煎子), compounding 주 (酒, 'wine, liquor'), 전 (煎, 'boil, heat, decoct'), and 자 (子, utensil suffix), originally naming a spouted metal pot for warming wine and later generalized to any kettle or teapot.

준비.etymology: Sino-Korean 준비 (準備), compounding 준 (準, 'level, standard, prepare') and 비 (備, 'prepare, provide, equip').

준비되다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 준비 (準備, 'preparation') + the native passive/inchoative verb 되다 ('to become, be made').

준비하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 준비 (準備, 'preparation') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, make').

준호.etymology: Korean masculine given name of Sino-Korean origin, typically written with hanja combinations such as 俊浩 or 準鎬 (compounding 준 俊 'talented, outstanding' or 準 'standard, level' with 호 浩 'vast, grand' or 鎬 'bright, shining').

줄.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 줄 ('cord, rope, string, line, row').

history.meaning: rope, string, cord, line, queue; bound noun for ability/fact ('how to, that')

줄기.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 줄기 ('plant stem, stalk, trunk; mountain ridge or stream'), derived from 줄 ('line, cord').

history.meaning: stem, stalk, continuous line or stream
stem, stalk, trunk; stream, ray, main thread

줄자.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 줄 ('string, cord, flexible strip') + 자 ('ruler, measuring rod', Middle Korean 자).

중간.etymology: Sino-Korean 중간 (中間), compounding 중 (中, 'middle, center') and 간 (間, 'space, interval, between').

중요하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 중요 (重要, 'importance, weightiness', compounding 重 'heavy, weighty' and 要 'essential, vital') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

즐겁다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 즐겁다 ('to be joyful, happy, pleasant'), derived from the verb stem 즐기- ('to enjoy, take pleasure in') + the adjectival suffix -업-.

history.meaning: to be pleasant, joyful, enjoyable, happy

지각하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 지각 (遲刻, 'being late for an appointed time, tardiness', compounding 遲 'slow, late' and 刻 'appointed time, moment') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: arriving past the appointed time, tardiness
to be late (for school, work, or an appointment)

지금.etymology: Sino-Korean 지금 (只今), compounding 지 (只, 'only, just') and 금 (今, 'now, the present'), attested since Middle Korean for 'right now, the present time'.

지나가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지나다 ('to pass by, cross, elapse') + the directional verb 가다 ('to go').

history.meaning: to pass by, go past, blow over

지나다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 디나다 ('to pass through, cross over, elapse'), with regular early Modern Korean palatalization of initial 디- to 지-.

지나다니다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지나다 ('to pass by') + 다니다 ('to go back and forth, walk around, commute').

history.meaning: to pass by regularly, walk or travel back and forth past a place

지난겨울.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 지난 ('past, last', past adnominal participle of 지나다 'to pass') + 겨울 ('winter', Middle Korean 겨슬 / 겨을).

지난주.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 지난 ('past, last', past adnominal participle of 지나다 'to pass') + Sino-Korean 주 (週, 'week').

지루하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 지리ᄒᆞ다 ('to be long and drawn-out, tedious, wearisome'), evolving through 지류하다 to modern 지루하다.

지붕.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 집우희 / 지븡 ('roof'), historically a compound of 집 ('house') and 우희 / 우 ('top, upper part', modern 위), literally 'the top of the house'.

지시하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 지시 (指示, 'pointing out, instruction, direction', compounding 指 'finger, point' and 示 'show, indicate') + the native light verb 하다.

지워지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 지우다 ('to erase, wipe away, blot out') + the auxiliary passive construction -어지다 ('to become, come to be').

history.meaning: to be erased, rub off, fade away

지켜보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 지키다 ('to guard, watch over') + 보다 ('to look at, see, watch').

history.meaning: to watch closely, keep an eye on, observe

지키다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 디키다 ('to guard, protect, watch over, keep'), with regular palatalization of initial 디- to 지-.

history.meaning: to protect, guard, keep (a promise or rule)

지퍼.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from American English zipper ('interlocking slide fastener').

지하실.etymology: Sino-Korean 지하실 (地下室), formed from 지하 (地下, 'underground, below the ground', from 地 'earth, ground' + 下 'below, under') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

지훈.etymology: Korean masculine given name of Sino-Korean origin, commonly written with hanja such as 智勳 or 志勳 (compounding 지 智 'wisdom' or 志 'noble will, ambition' with 훈 勳 'meritorious achievement').

직원.etymology: Sino-Korean 직원 (職員), compounding 직 (職, 'office, post, duty, occupation') and 원 (員, 'member, personnel').

직접.etymology: Sino-Korean 직접 (直接), compounding 직 (直, 'straight, direct, immediate') and 접 (接, 'touch, contact, meet').

직조.etymology: Sino-Korean 직조 (織造), compounding 직 (織, 'weave, knit') and 조 (造, 'make, manufacture').

진실.etymology: Sino-Korean 진실 (眞實), compounding 진 (眞, 'true, genuine, real') and 실 (實, 'fruit, substance, reality, fact').

진정하다.etymology: Represents two Sino-Korean formations: as a verb ('to calm down, settle, subside'), from 진정 (鎭靜, 'quelling and quieting', from 鎭 'press down, pacify' + 靜 'quiet, still') + 하다; as an adjective ('to be genuine, true'), from 진정 (眞正, 'true and right') + 하다.

history.meaning: to calm down, compose oneself; to be genuine, true

진짜.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 진 (眞, 'true, real, genuine') + the native/bound suffixoid -짜 ('article, item, person of a given quality'; compare 가짜 'fake').

history.meaning: genuine article, real thing; really, truly

진하다.etymology: Attested in Middle Korean as 진ᄒᆞ다 ('to be thick, viscous, deep in color or flavor'), formed from Sino-Korean 진 (津, 'sap, rich fluid', or 眞 'pure, concentrated') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be dark (in color), strong/rich (in flavor or scent), thick, deep

진회색.etymology: Compound formed from 진- ('dark, deep', root of 진하다) + Sino-Korean 회색 (灰色, 'gray color', from 灰 'ash' + 色 'color').

짐.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 짐 ('load carried on the back or head, pack, burden'), related to the verb 지다 ('to carry on the back').

history.meaning: that which is carried on the back, load, pack

집.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 집 ('house, home, dwelling, family; protective case or sheath').

집다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 집다 ('to pick up with the fingers, chopsticks, or tongs; to pinch').

history.meaning: to pick up, pluck, point out

집세.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 집 ('house, home') + Sino-Korean 세 (貰, 'rent, lease payment, hire').

짝.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 짝 / 쨕 ('one of a pair, partner, mate, matching half').

history.meaning: mate, partner, one of a pair

짧다.etymology: Native Korean adjective descending from Middle Korean 뎌르다 / 쟑다 ('to be short in length or duration').

짭짤하다.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated taste adjective formed from the root of 짜다 ('to be salty', Middle Korean ㅭᆞ다 / 짜다) + the adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be pleasantly salty, savory; to be tidy/lucrative (of income)

쪽.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 쯼 / 쪽 ('split half, piece, slice; side, direction').

history.meaning: direction, side, way; page; piece, clove

쪽지.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 쪽 ('small piece, slip, fragment') + Sino-Korean 지 (紙, 'paper').

history.meaning: small slip of paper, short note, memo

쭉.etymology: Native Korean mimetic/ideophonic adverb expressing straight, uninterrupted extension in space or time ('straight through, all the way, in a row, in one draught').

history.meaning: straight, continuously, all the way, in one gulp

찌푸리다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from early Modern Korean 쯰푸리다 / 찌푸리다 ('to knit one's brows, frown; for the weather to become overcast').

history.meaning: to frown, grimace, scowl; to become overcast

찍히다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb formed from 찍다 ('to stamp, imprint, dot, take a picture, chop') + the passive suffix -히-.

history.meaning: to be stamped, be imprinted, be photographed, be singled out

찡그리다.etymology: Native Korean verb ('to wince, grimace, screw up one's face or eyes') attested since early Modern Korean, expressively related to 찌푸리다 ('to frown').

history.meaning: to screw up one's face, wince

찢어지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 찢다 ('to tear, rip, rend', Middle Korean 찟다) + the auxiliary passive construction -어지다.

history.meaning: to be torn, get ripped, split apart

차.etymology: Represents two core Sino-Korean nouns borrowed from Middle Chinese: 차 (車, 'wheeled vehicle, cart, car, train') and 차 (茶, 'tea'); also represents 차 (差, 'difference, gap') and 차 (次, 'order, next, for the purpose of').

history.form: 車 / 茶 / 差 / 次 (차)
history.meaning: vehicle, carriage / tea / difference / order, occasion
car, vehicle; tea; difference; bound noun for purpose/occasion

차갑다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective derived from the stem of 차다 ('to be cold, icy', Middle Korean ᄎᆞ다) + the adjectival suffix -갑-.

history.meaning: to be cold to the touch, chilly, cold-hearted

차다.etymology: Convergence of several native Korean verbs and adjectives from Middle Korean: (1) 츠다 > 차다 ('to kick'), (2) ᄎᆞ다 > 차다 ('to become full, be filled'), (3) ᄎᆞ다 > 차다 ('to be cold, icy'), and (4) ᄎᆞ다 > 차다 ('to wear or fasten at the waist or wrist').

history.meaning: to kick / to be full; to be cold; to wear at the waist
to kick; to be full; to be cold; to wear (a watch or belt)

차례.etymology: Sino-Korean 차례 (次例), compounding 차 (次, 'order, sequence, next') and 례 (例, 'rule, custom, precedent'); homophonous with 차례 (茶禮, 'traditional holiday ancestral memorial rite').

history.meaning: order, turn, table of contents; ancestral rite

차림.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun formed from 차리다 ('to prepare, set out, dress up, equip') + the substantive suffix -ㅁ.

history.meaning: dress, attire, outfit; table setting or preparation

차분하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective formed from the root 차분- ('calm, settled, composed') + the adjective-forming verb 하다.

history.meaning: to be calm, composed, quiet and steady

차지하다.etymology: Formed from 차지 ('taking possession, share, charge', attested in Joseon administrative usage as 차디 次知 'person in charge, custody') + the native light verb 하다.

history.meaning: to occupy, take possession of, win, account for

찬물.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 찬 ('cold', adnominal participle of 차다 'to be cold', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆫ) + 물 ('water', Middle Korean 믈).

참.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ ('truth, reality; truly, really, very'); also used as an interjection upon sudden recollection ('oh, by the way!').

참나무.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 참 ('true, genuine, fine', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ) + 나무 ('tree, wood', Middle Korean 나모), literally 'true tree', designating oak trees (genus Quercus).

찻잔.etymology: Compound of Sino-Korean 차 (茶, 'tea') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 잔 (盞, 'cup').
