찻잔.notes: Written with linking ㅅ because both nouns are established monosyllabic Sino-Korean roots acting like native compounds.

찻주전자.etymology: Sino-Korean compound formed from 차 (茶, 'tea') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + 주전자 (酒煎子, 'spouted kettle or pot').

찻집.etymology: A compound of 차 'tea' and native 집 'house', joined by the linking ㅅ (사이시옷) written under 차.
찻집.notes: The same linking ㅅ appears in 찻잔 'teacup'.

창가.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 창 (窓, 'window') + native Korean 가 ('edge, border, side', Middle Korean ᄀᆞᆺ).

창고.etymology: Sino-Korean 창고 (倉庫), compounding 창 (倉, 'granary, storehouse') and 고 (庫, 'storehouse, depot, treasury').

창문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 창문 (窓門), joining 창 (窓, 'window') and 문 (門, 'door, opening').
창문.notes: Traditional Korean architecture built lattice windows that swing or slide like small doors, making 창문 completely natural.

창밖.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 창 (窓, 'window') + native Korean 밖 ('outside, exterior').

찾다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 찿다 ('to seek, look for, find, visit').

history.meaning: to look for, find, retrieve, visit

채.etymology: As a native Korean bound noun ('while still in the state of, just as it is'), descending from Middle Korean 채; also a native Korean counter for buildings or houses, blankets, and hand-pulled vehicles.

history.meaning: intact state, just as it is; counter for houses or curtains
while/with (state intact); counter for buildings; whip/rod

채소.etymology: Sino-Korean 채소 (菜蔬), compounding 채 (菜, 'edible greens, vegetables') and 소 (蔬, 'edible herbs, greens').

채우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb descending from Middle Korean 채오다 / 채우다, derived from 차다 ('to become full' and 'to wear/fasten').

history.meaning: to make full, fill; to fasten
to fill up, satisfy; to lock, button, or buckle

책.etymology: Sino-Korean 책 (冊, 'book, volume, register'), originally depicting bound bamboo or wooden writing slips in Old Chinese.

책상.etymology: Sino-Korean 책상 (冊床), compounding 책 (冊, 'book') and 상 (床, 'table, low platform, stand').

책장.etymology: Represents two Sino-Korean compounds: 책장 (冊欌, 'bookcase, bookshelf', from 冊 'book' + 欌 'cabinet, cupboard') and 책장 (冊張, 'page or leaf of a book', from 冊 'book' + 張 'sheet').

history.meaning: book cabinet / sheet of a book
bookcase, bookshelf; page of a book

챙기다.etymology: Native Korean verb attested since early Modern Korean as 챵기다 / 챙기다 ('to gather and pack tightly, make sure to take along; to look after').

history.meaning: to put in order, gather up, pack
to pack, remember to bring; to take care of, look after

처음.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 처섬 ('beginning, start, first time'), evolving through 처엄 to modern 처음 via loss of intervocalic ㅿ.

history.meaning: beginning, first time; for the first time

척.etymology: As a native Korean bound noun ('pretense, feigned air', used in -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다), attested since early Modern Korean (쳑 / 척); also Sino-Korean 척 (隻, counter for ships) and 척 (尺, traditional foot unit).

history.meaning: act of pretending (bound noun); counter for boats (隻)

척척.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated mimetic/ideophonic adverb describing actions carried out smoothly, briskly, and without a hitch ('smoothly, right away, one after another').

history.meaning: smoothly and promptly, without hesitation; sticking closely

척하다.etymology: Native Korean auxiliary verb formed from the bound noun 척 ('pretense, outward show') + the verb 하다 ('to do, make').

history.meaning: to pretend, feign, act as though

천.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 천 (千, 'one thousand'); homophonous with native Korean noun 천 ('woven cloth, fabric') and Sino-Korean 천 (天, 'sky, heaven').

천만다행.etymology: Sino-Korean four-character expression 천만다행 (千萬多幸), compounding 천만 (千萬, 'ten million, myriad, exceedingly') and 다행 (多幸, 'great good fortune, lucky', from 多 'much' + 幸 'fortune').

history.meaning: a stroke of immense good fortune
great relief, stroke of huge luck ('thank goodness')

천장.etymology: Sino-Korean 天障, literally the 'sky screen' above a room.

천천히.etymology: Attested in Middle and early Modern Korean as 쳔쳔히 ('slowly, unhurriedly'), formed from reduplicated 천천 (originally linked to Sino-Korean 儃儃 'leisurely, unhurried') + the native adverbial suffix -히.

철대문.etymology: Sino-Korean 철대문 (鐵大門), formed from 철 (鐵, 'iron, steel') + 대문 (大門, 'main gate of a house', from 大 'large, main' + 門 'gate, door').

철문.etymology: Sino-Korean 철문 (鐵門), compounding 철 (鐵, 'iron, steel') and 문 (門, 'door, gate').

철물점.etymology: Sino-Korean 철물점 (鐵物店), formed from 철물 (鐵物, 'ironware, hardware, metal tools', from 鐵 'iron' + 物 'articles, goods') + 점 (店, 'shop, store').

철사.etymology: Sino-Korean 철사 (鐵絲), compounding 철 (鐵, 'iron, steel') and 사 (絲, 'thread, filament, wire').

첫.etymology: Native Korean determiner descending from Middle Korean 첫 ('first, initial'), sharing a historical root with 처음 ('beginning, first time').

첫날.etymology: Native Korean compound formed from 첫 ('first') + 날 ('day', Middle Korean 날).

첫째.etymology: Native Korean ordinal numeral formed from 첫 ('first') + the ordinal suffix -째 ('-th in order').

체크인.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English check-in ('registration upon arrival at a hotel, airport, or venue').

history.meaning: arrival registration at a hotel or airport

체크인하다.etymology: Hybrid verb formed from the English loanword 체크인 (check-in) + the native Korean light verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to check in (at a hotel or airport)

쳐다보다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb contracted from 치어다보다, formed from 치- ('upward') + connective -어다 + 보다 ('to look, see').

history.meaning: to look upward at, gaze at
to look up at, look squarely at, stare at

초.etymology: Represents several common words: (1) native/nativized 초 ('candle', Middle Korean 초, early borrowing from Chinese 燭 'torch, candle'), (2) Sino-Korean 초 (秒, 'second of time'), (3) Sino-Korean 초 (初, 'beginning, early part'), and (4) Sino-Korean 초 (醋, 'vinegar').

history.form: 초 (< 燭) / 秒 / 初 / 醋 (초)

history.meaning: candle; second (unit of time); beginning of a period; vinegar

초록.etymology: Sino-Korean 초록 (草綠), compounding 초 (草, 'grass, plants') and 록 (綠, 'green'), literally 'grass green'.

초록색.etymology: Sino-Korean 초록색 (草綠色), formed from 초록 (草綠, 'grass green') + 색 (色, 'color').

초벌칠.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean prefix 초- (初, 'first, initial') + native Korean 벌 ('round, layer, set') + Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, paint, coating').

history.meaning: first coat of paint or plaster, primer coat, undercoat

초인종.etymology: Sino-Korean three-character compound 초인종 (招人鐘): 초 (招, 'summon, invite') + 인 (人, 'person') + 종 (鐘, 'bell').
초인종.notes: Literally 'a bell for calling someone'—the everyday Korean word for a doorbell or room buzzer.

최고.etymology: Sino-Korean 최고 (最高), compounding the superlative prefix 최- (最, 'most, supreme') and 고 (高, 'high, tall, lofty').

추억.etymology: Sino-Korean 추억 (追憶), compounding 추 (追, 'follow back, retrace') and 억 (憶, 'remember, call to mind').

축배.etymology: Sino-Korean 축배 (祝杯), from 축 (祝, 'celebrate, felicitate') + 배 (杯, 'cup, goblet').
축배.notes: Idiomatic in 축배를 들다 ('raise a celebratory glass / celebrate victory').

축축해지다.etymology: Native Korean inchoative verb formed from the ideophonic adjective 축축하다 ('to be damp, moist, clammy') + the auxiliary construction -어지다 ('to become, grow').

history.meaning: to become damp, get moist or soggy

축하하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 축하 (祝賀, 'congratulation, celebration', compounding 祝 'pray for blessing, felicitate' and 賀 'congratulate, celebrate') + the native light verb 하다.

출입문.etymology: Sino-Korean 출입문 (出入門), formed from 출입 (出入, 'going out and coming in, entry and exit', from 出 'go out' + 入 'enter') + 문 (門, 'door, gate').

춤추다.etymology: Native Korean cognate-object compound verb descending from Middle Korean 춤츠다, formed from the verbal noun 춤 ('dance', from 추- + -ㅁ) and the verb 추다 ('to dance').

춥다.etymology: Native Korean p-irregular adjective descending from Middle Korean 춥다 ('to be cold [of weather, air, or one's body feeling the cold]').

충분하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 충분 (充分, 'fullness, sufficiency', compounding 充 'fill, full' and 分 'measure, share, portion') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

충분히.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 충분 (充分, 'sufficient, ample') + the native Korean adverbial suffix -히.

층.etymology: Sino-Korean 층 (層, 'story of a building, floor, tier, layer, stratum').

history.meaning: floor, story (of a building), layer, level

층계참.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from Sino-Korean 층계 (層階, 'stairs, flight of steps', from 層 'tier, story' + 階 'steps, stairs') + 참 ('resting stage, post station', Middle Korean ᄎᆞᆷ / 站), literally 'resting stage on a staircase'.

치다.etymology: Native Korean polysemous verb descending from Middle Korean 치다 ('to strike, hit, beat, play [an instrument], pitch [a tent or screen]') and 츠다 ('to raise animals; to prune branches').

history.meaning: to strike, beat, put up a screen / to rear, prune
to hit, strike, play, take (a test), draw (a curtain), raise (livestock)

치대다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from the prefix/verb stem 치- ('upward, hard, repeatedly') + 대다 ('to touch, press against, apply').

history.meaning: to knead vigorously, work dough; to rub or lean against

치수.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 치 ('Korean inch, tenth of a 자', Middle Korean 치) + interfix -ㅅ- + Sino-Korean 수 (數, 'number, figure'), literally 'number of inches'.

치즈.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English cheese ('food made from pressed curds of milk').

친구.etymology: Sino-Korean 친구 (親舊), compounding 친 (親, 'intimate, close, relative') and 구 (舊, 'old, long-standing acquaintance').

history.meaning: relatives and old friends; close companion

친절.etymology: Sino-Korean 친절 (親切), compounding 친 (親, 'intimate, close, warm') and 절 (切, 'earnest, keen, thorough').

친해지다.etymology: Inchoative verb formed from 친하다 ('to be close, intimate', from Sino-Korean 親 'close, intimate' + 하다) + the auxiliary construction -어지다 ('to become, grow').

history.meaning: to become close friends, grow familiar with one another

칠.etymology: Sino-Korean numeral 칠 (七, 'seven'); homophonous with Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, varnish, coat of paint').

칠하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 칠 (漆, 'lacquer, varnish, paint') + the native light verb 하다 ('to do, apply').

history.meaning: to paint, coat, varnish, color in

칠호실.etymology: Sino-Korean 칠호실 (七號室), compounding 칠 (七, 'seven'), 호 (號, 'number, designation'), and 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

침대.etymology: Sino-Korean 침대 (寢臺), compounding 침 (寢, 'sleep, lie down') and 대 (臺, 'raised platform, stand, frame').

침착하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 침착 (沈着, 'composure, self-possession, steadiness', compounding 沈 'sink deep, settle' and 着 'attach, settle firmly') + the native adjective-forming verb 하다.

카드.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English card ('playing card, greeting card, identification or payment card').

history.meaning: stiff paper card, playing card, credit/debit card
card (greeting card, credit card, playing card)

카모마일.etymology: Borrowed from English chamomile ('aromatic daisy-like herb used in infusions', from Old French camomille < Late Latin chamomilla < Ancient Greek χαμαίμηλον 'earth-apple').

카운터.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English counter ('long service table or checkout desk in a shop, hotel, or restaurant; counting device').

history.meaning: service desk, checkout counter; counting device

카운트다운.etymology: Borrowed from English countdown ('backward counting of time to zero preceding a launch or event').

카페.notes: Modern Seoul neighbourhood word for coffeehouses and bakery cafés, largely superseding the mid-20th-century 다방 (茶房).

카펫.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English carpet ('thick woven floor covering').

칸.etymology: Nativized aspirated form of Sino-Korean 간 (間, 'space between two pillars, architectural bay, compartment, room'), attested since Middle Korean as 칸 / 간.

history.meaning: compartment, booth, section, blank space or square

칸막이.etymology: Compound formed from 칸 ('compartment, room section' < 間) + 막이 ('partition, screen, blocker', derived from 막다 'to block, divide' + nominalizer -이).

커드.etymology: Borrowed from English curd ('coagulated milk solids or thickened fruit spread such as lemon curd').

history.meaning: coagulated milk curd; creamy fruit spread

커버.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English cover ('protective casing, slipcover, lid, or musical cover version').

커튼.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English curtain ('hanging cloth screen for a window or stage').

커피.etymology: Borrowed from English coffee, adapted to Korean phonology with ㅋ (k) for initial c and ㅍ (p) for English f (since Korean lacks a labiodental fricative).
커피.notes: Replaced the older late-19th-century phonetic transcription 가배 (珈琲) in modern Korean.

커피잔.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from the English loanword 커피 (coffee) + Sino-Korean 잔 (盞, 'cup').

컴퓨터.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English computer ('programmable electronic computing machine').

컵.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English cup ('drinking vessel, glass, mug').

케이크.etymology: Borrowed from English cake, adding epenthetic 으 (-크) because Korean syllables do not end in an aspirated ㅋ release.
케이크.notes: Often shortened in casual speech to 케익, though 케이크 is the standard spelling.

켜다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean 혀다 ('to light a lamp or fire; to pull, saw wood, play a bowed instrument'), which underwent palatalization and aspiration (혀다 > 켜다).

history.meaning: to light (a fire/lamp); to pull, saw
to turn on, switch on, light (a lamp or appliance); to saw or play strings

켜지다.etymology: Native Korean passive/inchoative verb formed from 켜다 ('to light, turn on, switch on') + the auxiliary passive construction -어지다.

history.meaning: to be turned on, come on, light up

켤레.etymology: Native Korean classifier/counter for pairs of footwear, socks, or gloves, attested since early Modern Korean as 켤네 / 켤레.

history.meaning: counter for a pair of shoes or socks

코.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 고 (고ㅎ, an h-final noun meaning 'nose, snout, spout, tip'), which acquired initial aspiration from the internal *h* (고ㅎ > 코).

history.meaning: nose; spout; stitch loop in knitting

코트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English coat ('outer garment, overcoat', from Old French cote) and court ('enclosed sports playing area', from Old French cort).

크다.etymology: Native Korean adjective and verb descending from Middle Korean 크다 ('to be big, large, great; to grow up').

history.meaning: to be large, great; to grow
to be big, large, loud; to grow

크림색.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from English loanword 크림 (from English cream, ultimately from Old French cresme) + Sino-Korean 색 (色, 'color, tint').

큰길.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 큰 (adnominal form of 크다 'to be big, wide') + 길 ('road, street, way', Middle Korean 길).

큰일.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 큰 (adnominal form of 크다 'big, great, serious') + 일 ('work, matter, affair, event', Middle Korean 일).

클립.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English clip ('fastener for holding papers or hair together; video excerpt', from Old English clyppan 'to embrace, clasp').

클립보드.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English clipboard ('writing board with a hinged clip at the top; temporary software buffer'), compound of clip + board.

history.meaning: board with a spring clip; memory buffer

키.etymology: Two main sources merged under the same form: (1) native Korean 키 ('stature, height of a person; winnowing basket; helm/rudder', Middle Korean 키); (2) 20th-century loanword from English key ('metal key, keypad button, musical key').

키우다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 크다 ('to be big, grow', Middle Korean 크다 -> 키우다 / 틔우다) with the causative suffix -이우- / -우-.

history.meaning: to raise, bring up, cultivate, enlarge

킬로.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from French or English kilo, clipping of kilogramme / kilogram or kilomètre / kilometer (from Greek chilioi 'thousand').

타다.etymology: Multiple native Korean homophonous verbs descending from distinct Middle Korean roots: (1) 타다 ('to burn, catch fire, be scorched', Middle Korean 타다); (2) 타다 ('to ride, get on a vehicle', Middle Korean 타다); (3) 타다 ('to receive a share/prize; to mix/dissolve in liquid').

history.meaning: to burn; to mount/ride; to receive
to burn; to ride/board; to blend into water; to receive

타르트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from French tarte or English tart ('open-topped pastry shell with sweet or savory filling', ultimately from Old French tarte).

타르트지.etymology: Hybrid culinary compound formed from 타르트 ('tart', from French tarte / English tart) + Sino-Korean 지 (地, used in culinary terminology via Japanese kiji 生地 for 'dough base, pastry crust, fabric').

타이머.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English timer ('clockwork or electronic device that measures elapsed time or triggers an action', from time + -er).

타이어.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English tire / tyre ('rubber covering fitted around a wheel rim').

탁월하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 탁월 (卓越, 'standing out high above others, excellence', from 탁 卓 'tall, lofty, eminent' + 월 越 'to cross over, surpass') + native light verb 하다 ('to be').

history.meaning: lofty and surpassing -> to be outstanding, excellent

탁자.etymology: Sino-Korean 탁자 (卓子), compounding 탁 (卓, 'high table, stand') and diminutive/nominal suffix 자 (子, 'object, piece of furniture', from Middle/Early Mandarin 桌子 zhuōzi).

탄산수.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 탄산수 (炭酸水), formed from 탄산 (炭酸, 'carbonic acid', from 탄 炭 'charcoal, carbon' + 산 酸 'acid') + 수 (水, 'water').

탄탄하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the reduplicated bright-vowel mimetic root 탄탄 ('firm, solid, tightly built', vowel-harmonic counterpart of 튼튼하다) + -하다.

탓.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 탓 ('cause, reason, fault, blame').

태블릿.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th–early 21st century from English tablet ('flat slab, drawing pad, portable touchscreen computer', ultimately from Old French tablete, diminutive of Latin tabula).

태연하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 태연 (泰然, 'calm, composed, undisturbed', from 태 泰 'great, peaceful, tranquil' + 연 然 'manner, -ly') + native adjective suffix -하다.

택시.etymology: Borrowed from English taxi, preserving both syllables as 택 (taek) + 시 (si).
택시.notes: Pairs with the native verb 타다 ('택시를 타다', 'take a taxi') and 잡다 ('hail a taxi').

터지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb formed from 터 (bound root related to 트다 'to burst open, crack, sprout', Middle Korean 트다) + inchoative/passive auxiliary -어지다 ('to become, come to be').

history.meaning: to burst, pop, explode, break out

털다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 털다 ('to shake off dust or particles, beat out, empty out').

history.meaning: to shake off, knock dust from
to dust off, shake out, empty, rob

텅.etymology: Native Korean mimetic/ideophonic adverb expressing the state of a large space or hollow interior being completely empty (commonly in 텅 비다 'to be completely empty').

테.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 테 ('hoop, rim, frame, border bound around a barrel, wheel, or eyeglasses').

테이블.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English table ('piece of furniture with a flat top supported by legs; data chart', from Old French table, Latin tabula).

테이프.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English tape ('narrow strip of cloth, adhesive plastic, or magnetic recording ribbon', from Old English tæppe).

토마토수프.etymology: Compound loanword formed from 토마토 ('tomato', from English tomato) + 수프 ('soup', from English soup).

토스트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English toast ('sliced bread browned by radiant heat; toasted sandwich', from Old French toster, Latin torrere 'to parch, roast').

토요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 토요일 (土曜日), combining 토 (土, 'earth / Saturn'), 요 (曜, 'celestial luminary'), and 일 (日, 'day').
토요일.notes: Part of the traditional East Asian seven-luminaries week cycle adopted into modern Korean calendar usage.

통.etymology: Sino-Korean noun and counter: (1) 통 (桶, 'tub, barrel, bucket, cylindrical container', from Middle Chinese *duwngX); (2) 통 (通, 'counter for letters, phone calls, or documents; whole/entirety').

history.meaning: wooden tub, barrel, container; counter for letters/calls
container, bin, barrel; counter for letters/calls

통지서.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 통지서 (通知書), formed from 통지 (通知, 'notification, notice', from 통 通 'to communicate, pass through' + 지 知 'to know, inform') + 서 (書, 'written document').

통하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 통 (通, 'to pass through, communicate, circulate, be understood') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to pass through, lead to, communicate
to go through, circulate, make oneself understood, flow

튀기다.etymology: Native Korean causative verb derived from 튀다 ('to spring, bounce, splatter, pop', Middle Korean 튀다) + causative suffix -기- ('to make splatter/pop; to deep-fry in hot oil').

history.meaning: to cause to bounce/splatter -> to deep-fry in oil

트럭.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from American English truck ('motor vehicle designed to carry freight').

특급.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 특급 (特急), shortened from 특별 급행 (特別急行, 'special express') or 特級 ('special grade').
특급.notes: Widely used on express trains and courier vans (특급 배달, 'express delivery').

튼튼하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the reduplicated dark-vowel mimetic root 튼튼 ('sturdy, strong, robust, durable', heavy-vowel counterpart of 탄탄하다) + -하다.

틀리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 틀다 ('to twist, wind, turn awry', Middle Korean 틀다) + passive suffix -리-, literally 'to be twisted out of alignment' -> 'to go wrong, be incorrect, be mistaken'.

history.meaning: to twist -> to be twisted, go awry

틈.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 틈 ('crack, gap, chink, spare moment'), nominalized with -ㅁ from the verb 트다 ('to split open, crack, chap').

history.meaning: to crack open -> crack, opening, gap

티타임.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English tea time / teatime ('afternoon break for drinking tea and light refreshments', from tea + time).

history.meaning: time for afternoon tea; social break

파랗다.etymology: Native Korean color adjective descending from Middle Korean 파랗다 ('to be bright blue or vivid green'), bright-vowel harmonic counterpart of 퍼렇다, related to 풀 ('grass, vegetation') and 푸르다 ('to be blue/green').

history.meaning: to be bright blue or green
to be bright blue, azure (or pale with cold/fear)

파이.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English pie ('baked dish of fruit, meat, or sweet filling in a pastry crust') and from Greek/English pi (π, ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter).

파트너.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English partner ('associate in business, dance, sports, or marriage', from Anglo-Norman parcener, altered after part).

판.etymology: Sino-Korean and native Korean noun: (1) Sino-Korean 판 (板/版, 'wooden board, plank, printing block, edition'); (2) Sino-Korean/native 판 (局/場, 'scene, situation, round of a game or match', from Middle Korean 판).

history.meaning: flat board, plank, printing plate, edition
board, plate; round of a game, situation/arena

팔.etymology: Two homophonous Korean words: (1) Sino-Korean numeral 팔 (八, 'eight', from Middle Chinese *pɛt); (2) native Korean noun 팔 ('arm', Middle Korean ㅍᆞᆯ).

팔다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean ㅍᆞᆯ다 ('to sell, trade away').

팔리다.etymology: Native Korean passive verb derived from 팔다 ('to sell', Middle Korean ㅍᆞᆯ다) + passive suffix -리- ('to be sold, sell well; for one's attention to be distracted').

history.meaning: to be sold, be in demand; to be absorbed/distracted

팔십.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 팔십 (八十, 'eighty'), formed from 팔 (八, 'eight') + 십 (十, 'ten').

팔천.etymology: Sino-Korean compound numeral 팔천 (八千, 'eight thousand'), formed from 팔 (八, 'eight') + 천 (千, 'thousand').

팔호실.etymology: Sino-Korean compound noun 팔호실 (八號室, 'Room No. 8'), formed from 팔 (八, 'eight') + 호 (號, 'number, designation') + 실 (室, 'room, chamber').

팽팽하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the reduplicated mimetic root 팽팽 ('pulled taut, stretched tight, evenly matched') + adjective suffix -하다.

퍼뜨리다.etymology: Native Korean transitive/causative verb formed from the root 퍼- (from 펴다 'to spread out, unfold' / 퍼지다 'to spread') + intensive transitive suffix -뜨리- ('to spread widely, disseminate, circulate').

퍼센트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English percent ('parts per hundred, %', from Modern Latin per centum 'by the hundred').

펑.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic and mimetic adverb imitating a loud popping, bursting, or exploding sound, or describing a wide gap/hole opening suddenly.

페달.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English pedal or French pédale ('foot lever on a bicycle, car, piano, or machine', from Italian pedale, Latin pedalis 'of the foot').

페이지.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English page ('one side of a leaf of a book or document', from French page, Latin pagina).

history.meaning: leaf or side of a book

페인트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English paint ('liquid pigment coating applied to surfaces', from Old French peindre, Latin pingere).

페인트칠.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from English loanword 페인트 ('paint') + 칠 ('coating, varnishing, painting', from Sino-Korean 漆 'lacquer, varnish').

history.meaning: painting, applying a coat of paint

페인트칠하다.etymology: Compound verb formed from 페인트칠 ('applying paint', from English paint + 칠 漆 'coating') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to paint, apply a coat of paint

펠트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English felt ('non-woven textile produced by matting and pressing wool fibers', from Old English felt).

펴다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 펴다 ('to unfold, spread out, straighten, open').

편안하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 편안 (便安, 'comfortable and peaceful, well and at ease', from 편 便 'convenient, comfortable' + 안 安 'peaceful, tranquil') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: at ease and peaceful -> to be comfortable, peaceful

편지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 편지 (便紙), originally meaning 'handy/convenient note paper or message sent by courier', from 편 (便, 'convenient, opportunity, messenger') + 지 (紙, 'paper'), attested in Middle Korean as 편지.

history.meaning: convenient paper note -> written letter, epistle

편하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 편 (便, 'convenient, comfortable, easy') + native adjective suffix -하다 ('to be').

편히.etymology: Derived adverb formed from Sino-Korean 편 (便, stem of 편하다 'to be comfortable, easy') + native adverbial suffix -히.

펼쳐지다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive/passive verb formed from 펼치다 ('to spread out, unfold, open wide') + auxiliary passive/inchoative construction -어지다 ('to become unfolded, stretch out before one's eyes').

history.meaning: to unfold, spread out, be staged

펼치다.etymology: Native Korean intensive transitive verb derived from 펴다 ('to unfold, spread out', Middle Korean 펴다) with the intensive verbal extension -ㄹ치- ('to spread wide open, unfold, display').

history.meaning: to unfold -> to spread out wide, open up
to unfold, spread out, open (a book/wings), wage/stage

평가원.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 평가원 (評價員 or 評價院), formed from 평가 (評價, 'evaluation, appraisal', from 평 評 'to criticize, judge' + 가 價 'value, price') + 원 (員 'staff member, evaluator, inspector' or 院 'institute, agency').

평소.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 평소 (平素), joining 평 (平, 'ordinary, level, peaceful, usual') and 소 (素, 'plain, unadorned, habitual, from the start').

평화롭다.etymology: Derived adjective formed from Sino-Korean 평화 (平和, 'peace, harmony', from 평 平 'level, calm' + 화 和 'harmony, peace') + native adjectival suffix -롭다 ('characterized by').

포기하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 포기 (抛棄, 'throwing away, abandonment, renunciation', from 포 抛 'to fling, cast aside' + 기 棄 'to abandon, discard') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

포장.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포장 (包裝), joining 포 (包, 'wrap, bundle') and 장 (裝, 'dress, pack, outfit').
포장.notes: Also used at Korean restaurants and bakeries in 포장해 주세요 ('please pack it to go').

포장지.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포장지 (包裝紙), formed from 포장 (包裝, 'wrapping, packaging', from 포 包 'to wrap' + 장 裝 'to dress, pack') + 지 (紙, 'paper').

포함.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 포함 (包含), joining 포 (包, 'to wrap, encompass, enclose') and 함 (含, 'to hold in the mouth, contain, include').

폭.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 폭 (幅, 'width of cloth, breadth, span; counter for hanging scrolls or paintings', from Middle Chinese *pjuwk).

폭신하다.etymology: Native Korean ideophonic adjective formed from the bright-vowel mimetic root 폭신 ('soft, cushiony, yielding gently under pressure', harmonic counterpart of 푹신하다) + adjective suffix -하다.

폭우.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 폭우 (暴雨), from 폭 (暴, 'violent, sudden, fierce') and 우 (雨, 'rain').
폭우.notes: Shares 폭 (暴, 'fierce') with 폭풍 (暴風, 'storm') and 폭설 (暴雪, 'heavy snowfall').

폭풍.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 폭풍 (暴風), combining 폭 (暴, 'fierce, violent') and 풍 (風, 'wind').
폭풍.notes: Pronounced [폭풍] with unreleased [ㄱ] before aspirated ㅍ.

표정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 표정 (表情), joining 표 (表, 'outer surface, to express, show') and 정 (情, 'feeling, emotion, state of mind').

history.meaning: expressing inner feeling on the surface

표지.etymology: Sino-Korean homophonous compounds: (1) 표지 (表紙, 'book cover', from 표 表 'outer surface' + 지 紙 'paper'); (2) 표지 (標/標識, 'sign, mark, road sign, emblem', from 표 標 'mark, sign' + 지 識 'to recognize, mark').

history.form: 表紙 (book cover) / 標識 (sign, mark)
history.meaning: outer paper cover; identifying sign or marker

푹.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb expressing deep immersion, sinking in softly, boiling thoroughly, or sleeping soundly (bright-vowel counterpart 폭).

풀리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 풀다 ('to untie, loosen, dissolve, solve', Middle Korean 플다) + passive suffix -리-.

history.meaning: to untie -> to come untied, loosen
to come untied, be solved, thaw, subside (of anger/fatigue)

품다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 품다 ('to hold in one's bosom, embrace, brood/incubate eggs, harbor a thought'), related to the noun 품 ('bosom, breast of a garment').

history.meaning: to hold in the bosom, brood over

품위.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 품위 (品位), joining 품 (品, 'grade, quality, character, article') and 위 (位, 'rank, standing, dignity').

history.meaning: official rank and grade -> personal dignity and refinement

퓨즈.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English fuse ('electrical safety device containing a low-melting wire; cord for igniting explosives', from Italian fuso / Latin fusus).

프랑스식.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from 프랑스 ('France', from French France) + Sino-Korean suffix -식 (式, 'style, manner, method').

프런트.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English front ('front desk or reception area of a hotel; forward part', from Old French front, Latin frons).

프로답다.etymology: Hybrid adjective formed from 프로 ('professional', clipping of English professional) + native Korean adjectival suffix -답다 ('worthy of, like a true ...').

history.meaning: to be truly professional, worthy of a pro

플러그.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English plug ('electrical connector with prongs; stopper, spark plug', from Middle Dutch plugge).

피아노.etymology: Borrowed from English/Italian piano (short for Italian pianoforte, 'soft-loud').
피아노.notes: Takes the native Korean verb 치다 ('피아노를 치다', 'to play the piano').

피우다.etymology: Native Korean causative/transitive verb derived from 피다 ('to bloom, blossom; for a fire to burn up', Middle Korean 피다) + causative suffix -우- ('to make bloom, kindle a fire, smoke tobacco, emit a scent').

history.meaning: to bloom, burn -> to make bloom, kindle
to blossom, light a fire, smoke, give off a scent

morphemes.meaning: to cause to bloom or burn

핀.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English pin ('slender pointed metal fastener, hairpin, badge, bowling pin', from Old English pinn, Latin pinna).

핀셋.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century (via Japanese pinsetto ピンセット) from Dutch pincet ('tweezers, small forceps'), itself borrowed from French pincette (diminutive of pince, from pincer 'to pinch').

필요.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 필요 (必要), joining 필 (必, 'certainly, inevitably, must') and 요 (要, 'important, essential, to demand, require').

필요하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 필요 (必要, 'necessity, requirement') + native Korean adjective suffix -하다 ('to be').

하긴.etymology: Colloquial contraction of 하기는 ('indeed, when one thinks of it, to be sure'), formed from the nominalized stem 하기 (from 하다 'to do, say') + contrastive topic particle -는.

history.meaning: indeed, come to think of it, after all

하나.etymology: Native Korean numeral descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞ나 (stem ㅎᆞ낳-, 'one, single unit').

하나하나.etymology: Native Korean reduplicated compound of 하나 ('one', Middle Korean ㅎᆞ나), meaning 'one by one, each and every one individually'.

history.meaning: each individual one, one by one

하늘.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 하〮늘〯 (stem 하늘ㅎ-, 'sky, heaven').

하다.etymology: Native Korean verb descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞ다 ('to do, make, say, think; to be'), the primary light verb and adjective-forming auxiliary in Korean.

하얗다.etymology: Native Korean color adjective descending from Middle Korean 하야〮ㅎᆞ다〮 ('to be pure, bright white'), bright-vowel harmonic counterpart of 허옇다, expanded from the root of 희다 ('to be white').

history.meaning: to be dazzlingly or pure white

하우스.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English house ('building, dwelling; plastic greenhouse via 비닐하우스; club/venue'), from Old English hūs.

하지만.etymology: Grammaticalized conjunction formed from 하지 (stem 하- of 하다 'to do, be so' + connective base -지) + concessive particle -만 (shortened from -마는 'even though, however'), literally 'it is so, but...'.

하하.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic interjection and mimetic adverb representing open-mouthed, cheerful laughter ('haha!').

학교.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 학교 (學校), joining 학 (學, 'to learn, study, learning') and 교 (校, 'schoolhouse, wooden enclosure, to examine').

한.etymology: Native Korean adnominal numeral ('one, a single, approximately') descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞᆫ, adnominal modifier form of ㅎᆞ나 ('one'). (A homophonous Sino-Korean prefix 한- 大/韓/漢 also occurs in compounds.)

한가운데.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from the intensive prefix 한- ('exact, right in the middle, great', Middle Korean 한-) + 가운데 ('middle, center', from Middle Korean 가온대).

history.meaning: the very center, right in the middle

한마디.etymology: Native Korean compound noun formed from 한 ('one', adnominal of 하나) + 마디 ('joint of bamboo, node; a phrase or word of speech', Middle Korean 마디).

history.meaning: a single word, a brief remark

한밤중.etymology: Hybrid Korean compound combining native intensifying prefix 한- ('dead centre, peak'), native 밤 ('night'), and Sino-Korean 중 (中, 'middle').
한밤중.notes: Parallel to 한낮 ('high noon') and 한겨울 ('midwinter').

한번.etymology: Hybrid compound formed from native Korean 한 ('one', adnominal of 하나) + Sino-Korean 번 (番, 'turn, time, occasion'); lexicalized as a single word when meaning 'once (at some point), as a try, really'.

history.meaning: one time -> once, give it a try

한참.etymology: Native Korean compound noun and adverb formed from 한 ('one, a full') + 참 ('stage, rest stop on a journey, interval of time', Middle Korean ㅊᆞᆷ).

history.meaning: one full stage/interval -> a good while, a long time
a long while, quite some time

한테.etymology: Native Korean colloquial dative/locative particle ('to, from, at [an animate being]'), contracted in Early Modern Korean from 한데 ('in the same place, together', from 한 'one, same' + 데 'place').

history.meaning: at the same place -> to/for (a person or animal)

할머니.etymology: Native Korean kinship noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 할미 / 할머니, formed from 한- / 할- ('big, great, venerable', adnominal of 크다/하다 'great') + 어미 / 어머니 ('mother').

할아버지.etymology: Native Korean kinship compound from 한-/할- ('great, big', from 하다 'to be great/many' in Middle Korean) + 아버지 ('father').

할인.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 할인 (割引, first popularized via Meiji Japanese waribiki 割引), joining 할 (割, 'to cut, divide, proportion') and 인 (引, 'to pull back, deduct, draw').

함께.etymology: Native Korean adverb descending from Middle Korean ㅎᆞᆷ끠 ('together, at the same time'), formed from ㅎᆞᆫ ('one, same') + 끠 (locative/temporal noun 'time, occasion', modern 때).

history.meaning: at one and the same time, together

함께하다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 함께 ('together', Middle Korean ㅎᆞᆷ끠) + 하다 ('to do, share').

함정.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 함정 (陷穽), joining 함 (陷, 'to sink, fall into, trap') and 정 (穽, 'pitfall, covered pit for catching wild beasts').

항상.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb and noun 항상 (恒常), joining 항 (恒, 'constant, perpetual, lasting') and 상 (常, 'always, ordinary, unchanging').

해.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 해〮 ('sun, sunlight, year'), from Old Korean *hɛ ('sun, year').

해머.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English hammer ('heavy striking tool with a metal head, sledgehammer, athletic throwing hammer', from Old English hamor).

햇볕.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 햇볕, formed from 해 ('sun') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + 볕 ('warmth of the sun, sunshine').

햇빛.etymology: Native Korean compound noun descending from Middle Korean 햇빛, formed from 해 ('sun') + genitive interfix -ㅅ- + 빛 ('light, radiance, color').

햇살.etymology: Transparent native Korean compound joining 해 ('sun') + 사이시옷 (-ㅅ-) + 살 ('rays, arrows, spokes').
햇살.notes: Evokes individual warm beams of sunlight streaming through a courtyard or window.

행운.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 행운 (幸運), from 행 (幸, 'good fortune, blessing') and 운 (運, 'revolving fate, luck').
행운.notes: Commonly paired with native verb 빌다 in 행운을 빌어요 ('wishing you good luck').

향기.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 향기 (香氣), joining 향 (香, 'fragrance, sweet smell, incense') and 기 (氣, 'air, breath, aura, vapor').

향하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 향 (向, 'to face toward, head toward, direction') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

허락하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 허락 (許諾, 'permission, consent', from 허 許 'to allow, grant' + 락/낙 諾 'to assent, promise') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

허브.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English herb ('aromatic or medicinal plant used in cooking, tea, or perfumery', from Old French herbe, Latin herba) and hub ('central connection point').

허전하다.etymology: Hybrid/native Korean adjective formed on Sino-Korean 허 (虛, 'empty, hollow, void') + expressive suffix -전- + -하다, describing a lonely, wistful sense of emptiness when something or someone is missing.

history.meaning: to feel empty, wistful, or missing something

헌.etymology: Native Korean adnominal determiner descending from Middle Korean 헌 ('old, worn-out, shabby, secondhand'), frozen past adnominal participle of 헐다 ('to wear out, become dilapidated, crumble', Middle Korean 헐다).

history.meaning: old, worn, used, secondhand (as in 헌 옷, 헌 책)

헝겊.etymology: Native Korean noun attested in Early Modern Korean as 헝겁 / 헝겊 ('piece or scrap of woven cloth, rag'), likely formed from 헌 ('worn, old, scrap') + 거죽/꺼풀 ('outer skin, layer, covering').

history.meaning: piece of cloth, rag, fabric patch

현.etymology: Sino-Korean homophonous nouns and prefixes: (1) 현 (絃/弦, 'bowstring, string of a musical instrument'); (2) 현 (現, 'present, current, existing'); (3) 현 (縣, 'county, prefecture').

현관.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현관 (玄關), originally a Zen Buddhist term meaning 'the mysterious gateway to profound truth' (from 현 玄 'profound, dark, subtle' + 관 關 'barrier, gate'), later applied to the entrance hall of a temple and finally any home's entryway/vestibule.

history.meaning: gateway to profound mystery -> temple entrance hall

현관문.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현관문 (玄關門), formed from 현관 (玄關, 'entranceway, foyer') + 문 (門, 'door, gate').

현금.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현금 (現金), joining 현 (現, 'present, on hand, ready') and 금 (金, 'gold, metal, money').

현대식.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 현대식 (現代式), formed from 현대 (現代, 'modern times, the present age', from 현 現 'present' + 대 代 'era, generation') + 식 (式, 'style, mode').

현명하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 현명 (賢明, 'wise and clear-sighted', from 현 賢 'worthy, virtuous, sagacious' + 명 明 'bright, clear, discerning') + native adjective suffix -하다.

history.meaning: sagacious and discerning -> to be wise

혈압.etymology: Sino-Korean medical compound 혈압 (血壓), joining 혈 (血, 'blood') and 압 (壓, 'pressure, to press down').

형.etymology: Sino-Korean noun 형 (兄, 'elder brother', from Middle Chinese *xjwæng), thoroughly naturalized into Korean kinship terminology as 'older brother (of a male)' or 'older male friend'. (Homophonous 형 型 means 'model, type, mold'.)

형님.etymology: Hybrid honorific kinship noun formed from Sino-Korean 형 (兄, 'elder brother') + native Korean honorific suffix -님.

형제.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 형제 (兄弟), joining 형 (兄, 'elder brother') and 제 (弟, 'younger brother').

호두나무.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from 호두 ('walnut', altered from Sino-Korean 호도 胡桃 'western/steppe peach', from 호 胡 'northern/western steppe peoples' + 도 桃 'peach') + native Korean 나무 ('tree, wood', Middle Korean 나모).

호실.etymology: Sino-Korean bound compound 호실 (號室), joining 호 (號, 'number, designation') and 실 (室, 'room, chamber'), attached after numerals to name a specific room number.

호텔.etymology: Borrowed from English hotel (ultimately French hôtel).
호텔.notes: Contrasts in scale with smaller neighbourhood 게스트하우스 ('guesthouses') and traditional 한옥 숙소.

혹시.etymology: Sino-Korean adverb 혹시 (或是), joining 혹 (或, 'perhaps, someone, by any chance') and 시 (是, 'this, to be right/so'); used in Korean to mean 'by any chance, perhaps, in case'.

history.meaning: by any chance, perhaps, just in case

혼자.etymology: Native Korean noun and adverb descending from Middle Korean 호〮오〮자〮 / 호올로 ('alone, by oneself'), derived from the numeral root ㅎᆞ올- / ㅎᆞᆫ- ('one, single, solitary').

홍차.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 홍차 (紅茶), literally 'red tea', from 홍 (紅, 'crimson, reddish') + 차 (茶, 'tea').
홍차.notes: East Asian languages name black tea after the warm reddish-amber colour of the brewed liquid rather than the dry leaves.

화나다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 화 (火, 'fire; fiery anger, wrath') + native Korean intransitive verb 나다 ('to arise, break out, come forth', Middle Korean 나다).

화내다.etymology: Hybrid compound verb formed from Sino-Korean 화 (火, 'fire; anger, temper') + native Korean transitive/causative verb 내다 ('to put forth, let out, produce', Middle Korean 내다).

history.meaning: to express anger, lose one's temper

화면.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 화면 (畫面), joining 화 (畫, 'picture, painting, image') and 면 (面, 'face, surface, plane').

history.meaning: picture plane; television, monitor, or phone screen

화분.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 화분 (花盆), joining 화 (花, 'flower, flowering plant') and 분 (盆, 'basin, earthen pot, bowl').

화살표.etymology: A compound of native Korean 화살 'arrow' and Sino-Korean 표 (標) 'mark, symbol'.
화살표.notes: The arrow drawn on signs, maps and plans.

화요일.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 화요일 (火曜日, 'day of Mars / Tuesday'), formed from 화요 (火曜, 'celestial luminary of Fire, the planet Mars', from 화 火 'fire' + 요 曜 'shining celestial body') + 일 (日, 'day').

화음.etymology: Sino-Korean 화음 (和音), compounding 화 (和, 'harmonize, blend') + 음 (音, 'sound, tone').
화음.notes: Standard musical term for two or more notes sounding simultaneously in harmony.

화이트보드.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English whiteboard ('glossy white board for non-permanent dry-erase markers', compound of white + board).

화해하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 화해 (和解, 'reconciliation, making peace', from 화 和 'harmony, peace' + 해 解 'to untie, resolve, loosen') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to reconcile, make up, make peace

확실히.etymology: Derived adverb formed from Sino-Korean 확실 (確實, stem of 확실하다 'to be certain, sure, definite', from 확 確 'firm, solid, certain' + 실 實 'true, real, substantial') + native adverbial suffix -히.

확인하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 확인 (確認, 'confirmation, verification', from 확 確 'firm, certain' + 인 認 'to recognize, acknowledge, verify') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

환기창.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 환기창 (換氣窓), formed from 환기 (換氣, 'ventilation, exchanging air', from 환 換 'to exchange, replace' + 기 氣 'air') + 창 (窓, 'window').

환불하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 환불 (還拂, 'returning a payment, refund', from 환 還 'to return, give back' + 불 拂 'to pay out, clear away') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

history.meaning: to refund, get or give a refund

환영하다.etymology: Formed from Sino-Korean 환영 (歡迎, 'joyful reception, welcome', from 환 歡 'joyous, glad' + 영 迎 'to go out to meet, greet, receive') + native verb 하다 ('to do').

환하다.etymology: Native/Sino-Korean adjective attested in Middle Korean as 환ㅎᆞ다 ('to be bright, clear, open and wide; to be well-versed in'), traditionally linked either to a native mimetic root 환- ('bright, open') or Sino-Korean 환 (煥, 'shining, brilliant').

history.meaning: to be bright, luminous, wide open
to be bright, well-lit, radiant; to know inside out

활짝.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb expressing the manner of a door, window, flower, or smile opening wide, brightly, and completely (bright-vowel counterpart of 훌쩍).

history.meaning: wide open, in full bloom, beamingly

황금빛.etymology: Hybrid compound uniting Sino-Korean 황금 (黃金, 'yellow gold') with native Korean 빛 ('light, gleam, colour').
황금빛.notes: Korean productively attaches native 빛 to nouns to describe warm luminous hues (보랏빛, 은빛, 황금빛).

황동.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 황동 (黃銅), joining 황 (黃, 'yellow') and 동 (銅, 'copper, bronze'), literally 'yellow copper' (i.e. brass, an alloy of copper and zinc).

회색.etymology: Sino-Korean compound 회색 (灰色), joining 회 (灰, 'ash, ashes') and 색 (色, 'color').

회색빛.etymology: Hybrid compound noun formed from Sino-Korean 회색 (灰色, 'ash color, gray') + native Korean 빛 ('light, hue, tint, color', Middle Korean 빛).

후기.etymology: Sino-Korean homophonous compounds: (1) 후기 (後記, 'postscript, afterword, user/customer review written after an experience', from 후 後 'after, behind' + 기 記 'record, note'); (2) 후기 (後期, 'latter period, late phase', from 후 後 'later' + 기 期 'period').

history.form: 後記 (postscript, review) / 後期 (latter period)

훌륭하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective attested in Early Modern Korean as 훌융하다 / 훌륭하다 ('to be splendid, admirable, excellent, fine'), derived from an expressive root 훌륭.

history.meaning: to be excellent, great, admirable, fine

훨씬.etymology: Native Korean emphatic degree adverb descending from Early Modern Korean 훨씬 / 훨신 ('by far, much more'), related to the mimetic root 훨- ('broadly, freely, surpassing bounds').

history.meaning: much, far, a great deal (with comparatives)

휴.etymology: Native Korean onomatopoeic interjection imitating the sound of a long exhalation or sigh of relief ('phew!, whew!').

흐르다.etymology: Native Korean intransitive verb descending from Middle Korean 흐르다 ('for water or liquid to flow, run; for time to elapse').

흐릿하다.etymology: Native Korean adjective derived from 흐리다 ('to be cloudy, murky, dim, indistinct', Middle Korean 흐리다) + approximative/attenuative suffix -ㅅ하다 ('somewhat dim, blurry, hazy').

history.meaning: to be blurry, hazy, faint, indistinct

흑백.notes: Used for old photos and films, and figuratively for right and wrong.

흔들다.etymology: Native Korean transitive verb descending from Middle Korean 흔들다 ('to shake, wave, rock, sway back and forth').

흔들리다.etymology: Native Korean passive/intransitive verb derived from 흔들다 ('to shake, rock', Middle Korean 흔들다) + passive suffix -리- ('to be shaken, sway, wobble, waver').

history.meaning: to shake, sway, wobble, waver in resolve

흔들림.etymology: Native Korean verbal noun derived from 흔들리다 ('to shake, sway, waver', passive of 흔들다) + nominalizing suffix -ㅁ.

흘러가다.etymology: Native Korean compound verb formed from 흐르다 ('to flow', conjugated stem 흘러-) + directional auxiliary verb 가다 ('to go away'), meaning 'to flow along, drift away, pass by (of time)'.

history.meaning: to flow away, stream along, pass by

흙.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 흙 (dialectal/archaic 훍, 'earth, soil, dirt, clay').

흠뻑.etymology: Native Korean mimetic adverb expressing the state of being thoroughly soaked, drenched, or abundantly filled with moisture or emotion.

흥얼거리다.etymology: Native Korean iterative verb formed from the onomatopoeic root 흥얼 ('humming or murmuring a tune under one's breath') + repetitive verbal suffix -거리다 ('to keep doing').

history.meaning: to hum a tune, croon softly to oneself

힘.etymology: Native Korean noun descending from Middle Korean 힘 ('physical strength, power, force, effort; sinew').

힘껏.etymology: Native Korean derived adverb formed from 힘 ('strength, power', Middle Korean 힘) + suffix -껏 ('to the utmost limit of').

history.meaning: with all one's might, as hard as one can

힘차게.etymology: Native Korean adverbial form of the compound adjective 힘차다 ('to be full of strength, vigorous, powerful, energetic', from 힘 'strength' + 차다 'to be full, filled with') + adverbial ending -게.

history.meaning: full of strength -> vigorously, powerfully, energetically
